title: THE FIRST FRAME
goal: Catch the first thought before it expands into a whole story.
steps:
1. Trigger — A trigger flickers.
2. Pause Story — Do not explain it yet.
3. Capture Thought — Pin the first thought, picture, or prediction exactly as it arrived.
4. Quote — Put quotation marks around it.
5. Close Capture — The catch ends there; no life story, no courtroom, no spiral.
win: The trigger was captured exactly once without becoming a life story, trial, or spiral.
supports:
• Test the assumption; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Separate possibility from probability; ask what would change your mind.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; notice absolute words like always.
• Separate guess from evidence; check another angle.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check what you actually know.
formula_flow: Trigger → Pause Story → Capture Thought → Quote → Close Capture
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if holding the thought in mind makes you feel less steady or more upset.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE TWO-TRAY TEST
goal: Weigh visible facts on both sides before deciding what they mean.
steps:
1. Imagine Trays — Imagine two trays.
2. Name Sides — Name the left SUPPORTS IT and the right DOESN’T FIT.
3. Sort Facts — Drop only visible facts into them—no feelings disguised as evidence.
4. Switch Sides — Now cover the fuller tray and read the neglected one silently.
5. Balance Verdict — Finish with a verdict that can hold both sides without pretending they weigh the same.
win: Your verdict included supporting evidence and the facts your feeling had been overlooking.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; notice what changed physically.
• Do one steadying action; lower nearby noise.
• Name the feeling plainly; check the facts separately.
• Slow physical pace; give the feeling time to move.
• Check basic needs; name the emotion.
formula_flow: Imagine Trays → Name Sides → Sort Facts → Switch Sides → Balance Verdict
safety:
PAUSE
Stop when you are recycling arguments instead of discovering evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WORST CASE, WITH EXITS
goal: Turn the feared ending into a realistic path through and beyond it.
steps:
1. Name Fear — Picture the feared ending in one line.
2. Build Exits — Under it build four rungs: WHAT HAPPENS; WHAT I DO NEXT; WHO OR WHAT HELPS; HOW RECOVERY COULD BEGIN.
3. Add Likely — Add a fifth rung for the outcome that is actually most likely.
4. Climb Route — Move through the five steps once in your mind.
5. Act Now — Then take the first coping action available now.
win: The worst case gained exits, support, recovery steps, and a more likely outcome before you acted.
supports:
• Question absolute words; check what you actually know.
• Test the assumption; check the whole situation.
• Check the base rate; use recent, concrete evidence.
• Ask what would change your mind; use current facts.
• Check another angle; delay the verdict.
formula_flow: Name Fear → Build Exits → Add Likely → Climb Route → Act Now
safety:
PAUSE
Do not run this alone for immediate danger, medical crisis, or trauma flooding.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE ODDS RECEIPT
goal: Revise a scary probability using real reference points and opposing evidence.
steps:
1. Score Odds — Give the prediction a number from 0 to 100.
2. Check Baseline — Find one real reference point: how often has this happened in similar situations.
3. Weigh Evidence — Notice one fact that raises the odds and another that lowers them.
4. Revise Odds — Pick a new number and remember it.
5. Follow Evidence — Act from the revision, not the original alarm.
win: Your second estimate differed from the alarm number because actual evidence had entered the calculation.
supports:
• Use current facts; check the whole situation.
• Look for one missing fact; check the base rate.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; delay the verdict.
• Question absolute words; use a real example.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; separate possibility from probability.
formula_flow: Score Odds → Check Baseline → Weigh Evidence → Revise Odds → Follow Evidence
safety:
PAUSE
End the count if numbers become reassurance checking or you cannot stop recalculating.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE GREY DIAL
goal: Find the evidence-based middle between two extreme verdicts.
steps:
1. Name Extremes — Name the two extremes your mind is using.
2. Build Scale — Build a 0–10 scale between them and say three real anchor points: 2, 5, and 8.
3. Place Today — Place today’s event where the evidence fits—not where the emotion shouts.
4. Choose Response — Choose a response matched to that exact setting.
win: The event landed at a specific point on the scale and your response matched that setting.
supports:
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check the whole situation.
• Test the assumption; separate guess from evidence.
• Ask what else could fit; question absolute words.
• Check the base rate; notice absolute words like always.
• Use current facts; delay the verdict.

title: BORROW THEIR MIRROR
goal: Judge yourself by the same evidence standard you would use for someone you trust.
steps:
1. Imagine Trusted — Imagine a trusted person bringing you the same facts.
2. Offer Allowances — Hold the questions you would ask them, the allowances you would make, and the evidence you would require before judging them.
3. Remove Name — Now remove their name.
4. Apply Page — Apply that page to yourself without adding a harsher clause.
win: The harsher self-clause disappeared, leaving the questions and allowances you would genuinely give another person.
supports:

• Question absolute words; look for one missing fact.
• Separate guess from evidence; ask what would disprove it.
• Check the base rate; separate possibility from probability.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; use a real example.

title: THREE WORLDS, ONE FACT
goal: Keep several explanations alive until new evidence separates them.
steps:
1. Keep Event — Keep the event fixed.
2. Invent — Invent three models for why it happened.
3. Predict Different — Each model must predict a different thing you could observe next.
4. Earliest — Notice the earliest observation that would separate them.
5. Speak Plurals — Until that evidence arrives, speak in plurals: possibilities, not prophecy.
win: One event produced multiple testable possibilities instead of a single prediction dressed as certainty.
supports:
• Check what you actually know; look for one missing fact.
• Ask what else could fit; separate possibility from probability.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; separate guess from evidence.
• Ask what would disprove it; use recent, concrete evidence.
• Delay the verdict; use current facts.
formula_flow: Keep Event → Invent → Predict Different → Earliest → Speak Plurals
safety:
PAUSE
Do not multiply theories when an urgent practical response is already clear.

title: THE OLD-RULE CONTRABAND FILE
goal: Keep one real exception that your negative self-story usually throws away.
steps:
1. Capture — Catch one event your negative self-story would normally delete.
2. Describe Happened — Say what happened, why it really does not fit the old rule, and which convenient excuse the rule will use to dismiss it.
3. Seal — Seal the entry in your mind as usable evidence and bring it back tomorrow once—no chanting.
win: A fact that contradicted the old rule stayed recorded even after you noticed its usual excuse.
supports:
• Add the missing context; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Use a real example; separate guess from evidence.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; check another angle.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; check what you actually know.
• Notice absolute words like always; separate possibility from probability.
formula_flow: Capture → Describe Happened → Seal
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use exceptions to deny real problems that need action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MAKE THE BELIEF BET
goal: Test a belief with a small action that could prove it wrong.
steps:
1. State Belief — State the belief as a clear prediction.
2. Choose Safe — Choose a safe, small action that could prove it wrong as well as right.
3. Picture Outcome — Picture the expected result before acting.
4. Test Observation — Run the test, then compare observation with prediction.
5. Pay Out — Pay out only to evidence.
win: Observation, not expectation, decided how the belief's prediction scored after the experiment.
supports:
• Test the assumption; ask what else could fit.
• Separate guess from evidence; question absolute words.
• Notice absolute words like always; use a real example.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; separate possibility from probability.
• Check the base rate; ask what would disprove it.
formula_flow: State Belief → Choose Safe → Picture Outcome → Test Observation → Pay Out
safety:
PAUSE
Cancel any experiment involving danger, coercion, medical risk, or another person’s consent.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FORECAST SCOREBOARD
goal: Track how confident predictions compare with what actually happens over time.
steps:
1. Count Hit — Before an uncertain event, remember four items: prediction, confidence %, deadline, and what counts as a hit.
2. Keep Result — Afterward, hold the result without rewriting the original entry.
3. Calculate — Calculate the gap between confidence and reality.
4. Spot the Bias — After five rounds, look for your recurring bias.
win: The original forecast stayed intact long enough to reveal the gap between confidence and reality.
supports:
• Stop planning after one action; begin with the easiest part.
• Set a two-minute timer; remove one barrier.
• Restart quickly; touch the first item.
• Lower standards briefly; prepare first.
• Choose a rough beginning; prepare the task in advance.
formula_flow: Count Hit → Keep Result → Calculate → Spot the Bias
safety:
PAUSE
Retire the ledger if it feeds compulsive monitoring.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE EFFORT STAIRCASE
goal: Start at the smallest task level that still leaves real evidence.
steps:
1. Name — Name five versions of the task from almost easy to genuinely stretching.
2. Remove Decoy — Mentally remove the zero-effort decoy.
3. Remain Version — Do the smallest remaining version that leaves visible evidence—one paragraph, one call, one plate washed.
4. Climb Stair — Next time, climb only one stair.
win: One visible piece of work existed, and the next challenge only needed to rise by one step.
supports:
• Restart quickly; stop planning after one action.
• Cut the task; prepare first.
• Remove one obvious distraction; start smaller.
• Reward starting, not finishing; start physically.
• Begin with the easiest part; lower the first demand.

title: MOOD HAS ALIBIS
goal: Compare predicted mood with what actually changes during real activities.
steps:
1. Choose Activity — Choose one activity.
2. Score Expected — Before it, score expected mood; at the start, notice your actual mood; at the end, score again.
3. Add Sentence — Add one sentence about what changed during the activity.
4. Try Three Ways — Repeat with three different actions before deciding ‘nothing helps.’
win: Several activities produced before-and-after evidence before the claim 'nothing helps' was allowed to stand.
supports:
• Lower stimulation for a minute; avoid decisions at peak emotion.
• Wait before sending messages; name the feeling plainly.
• Use plain language; separate feeling from fact.
• Do one steadying action; slow physical pace.
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; check basic needs.

title: TWO ENGINES
goal: Feed pleasure and mastery separately instead of asking one activity to fix everything.
steps:
1. Schedule Chosen — For the next day, schedule one act chosen purely for enjoyment and one chosen for competence.
2. Make Small — Make both small enough to happen.
3. Check Both — After each activity, ask which engine it fed: pleasure or mastery. Rate that one channel only.
4. Drop Demand — Do not demand that either activity fix everything.
win: One small enjoyable act and one competence-building act each delivered evidence to their own channel.
supports:
• Cut the task; start before you feel ready.
• Start with one minute; restart quickly.
• Do the easiest useful part; open only what you need.
• Start smaller; lower the quality bar.
• Start physically; make it visible.

title: MAKE THE ROOM VOTE
goal: Make the wanted behaviour easier to enter and the unwanted default harder to reach.
steps:
1. Pick Desired — Pick one desired behaviour and one unwanted default.
2. Picture Routes — Picture the desired route becoming easier and the unwanted route becoming slightly harder.
3. Add Friction — Imagine one extra decision appearing before the unwanted default can happen.
4. Let Choice Win — Mentally rehearse taking the easier desired route once.
win: The environment contained an extra pause before the old default and a smoother route toward the desired action.
supports:
• Open only what you need; start before you feel ready.
• Stop planning after one action; restart quickly.
• Use two minutes; choose tiny action.
• Set a two-minute timer; start physically.
• Make the first move tiny; begin while unsure.
formula_flow: Pick Desired → Picture Routes → Add Friction → Let Choice Win
safety:
PAUSE
Keep changes reversible and never block access to medication, food, safety, or essential contact.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET THE URGE MISS ITS APPOINTMENT
goal: Let an urge rise and fall without doing the usual ritual.
steps:
1. Name Cue — Name the cue and the usual calming act it normally summons.
2. Contact — Contact only a manageable dose of the cue.
3. Keep Hands — Keep your hands and attention out of the ritual while the urge changes on its own.
4. Mark Peak — Hold the peak and the first natural drop.
5. Let Learning Land — The learning comes from not doing the old ritual.
win: The urge changed on its own while the old calming act stayed undone.
supports:
• Remember urges peak and fall; use your hands.
• Move away from the cue; make access harder.
• Delay ten minutes; eat if hungry.
• Avoid bargaining; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Change rooms if possible; make access less convenient.
formula_flow: Name Cue → Contact → Keep Hands → Mark Peak → Let Learning Land
safety:
PAUSE
Use clinical guidance for severe OCD, addiction, eating disorders, or exposures that feel unsafe.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHEN/THEN FIRMWARE
goal: Turn one visible cue into one tiny automatic start.
steps:
1. Picture Line — Picture one line only: WHEN [specific visible cue], THEN I WILL [small physical action].
2. Remove Vague — Remove vague words such as try, soon, or better.
3. Imagine Cue — Imagine the cue once, do the action once, and place the rule where the cue occurs.
4. Skip Pep Talk — Skip the pep talk.
win: The cue appeared and the planned physical action happened without a pep talk.
supports:
• Start before you feel ready; open only what you need.
• Begin with the easiest part; use a visible cue.
• Choose a rough beginning; shrink the first action.
• Open the task; start smaller.
• Start with one minute; make the first move tiny.
formula_flow: Picture Line → Remove Vague → Imagine Cue → Skip Pep Talk
safety:
PAUSE
Rewrite the rule if the trigger is unclear or the response depends on another person.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FIRST DRIFT
goal: Catch the earliest drift before the full unwanted behaviour begins.
steps:
1. Picture the Path — Trace the unwanted behaviour backward in your mind: first act, private permission, routine change, environment shift, body state.
2. Mark Earliest — Place a red dot on the earliest sign you could realistically notice.
3. Plant Interrupt — Attach one simple interruption to that red dot and rehearse what you will do when it appears.
win: You identified one early red flag and attached a simple interruption to it.
supports:
• Use simple words for the problem; rest before deciding.
• Name the emotion; lower nearby noise.
• Use plain language; give the feeling time to move.
• Check the facts separately; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Notice what changed physically; check basic needs.
formula_flow: Picture the Path → Mark Earliest → Plant Interrupt
safety:
PAUSE
For substance withdrawal, overdose risk, or dangerous relapse, use medical and emergency support rather than self-management alone.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ADD THE PREFIX
goal: Notice the thought as mental activity, then keep doing what you chose.
steps:
1. Prefix Thought — Put “I am noticing my mind produce…” before the thought. Say the whole sentence once at normal speed.
2. Check Command — Notice what remains true and what loses command authority.
3. Resume Task — Carry on with the next chosen task while the sentence exists nearby.
win: The thought remained present without deciding what your hands or attention did next.
supports:
• Start physically; shrink the first action.
• Reward starting, not finishing; choose tiny action.
• Cut the task; make it visible.
• Skip extra setup; lower the first demand.
• Begin while unsure; choose a rough beginning.

safety:
PAUSE
Drop the wording if it feels mocking, unreal, or destabilising.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WORD MELT
goal: Hear one charged word as sound instead of carrying its whole story.
steps:
1. Choose Charged — Choose one charged word—not a whole painful story.
2. Say Gently — Say it gently and steadily for about twenty seconds.
3. Listen Moment — Listen for the moment it becomes rhythm, mouth movement, or noise.
4. Stop Room — Stop there and look around the room.
5. Return Seen — Meaning may return; you have seen it separate once.
win: For a moment, the word became rhythm or mouth movement before its meaning returned.
supports:
• Change one cue; make the new habit easier.
• Reset after slips; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Keep replacement easy; make the old habit harder.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; add small friction.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; reset without self-criticism.
formula_flow: Choose Charged → Say Gently → Listen Moment → Stop Room → Return Seen
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid this with slurs, trauma phrases, voices, or material that escalates symptoms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE BAD VOICE ACTOR
goal: Loosen a thought's authority by changing how its voice sounds.
steps:
1. Read Wrong — Hear the thought as a tired GPS, an overdramatic sports commentator, or a hesitant intern reading the wrong memo.
2. Keep Words — Keep the words unchanged; alter only tempo, pitch, and confidence.
3. Natural Voice — Then say it again in your natural voice as a possibility, not an order.
win: The same words felt more like a possibility once tone and confidence were altered.
supports:
• Separate possibility from probability; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Delay the verdict; look for one missing fact.
• Check another angle; ask what else could fit.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; test the assumption.
• Use current facts; add the missing context.
formula_flow: Read Wrong → Keep Words → Natural Voice
safety:
PAUSE
Use a neutral voice instead if playful recasting feels shaming or agitating.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE LIFE DIRECTION TEST
goal: Choose the next hour by direction, not by the loudest thought.
steps:
1. Picture — Picture two arrows.
2. Make Room — One shows the next hour if you obey the thought; the other reveals what unfolds over sixty minutes when you make room for it but follow a chosen value.

win: You could see which option moved toward a value even while uncertainty stayed present.
supports:
• Check whose goal; use values to choose trade-offs.
• Make the next hour reflect it; protect important time.
• Act before motivation; choose aligned action.
• Use one priority; do not wait for motivation.
• Review what the action costs; name today's value.

title: EDIT THE FONT, NOT YOURSELF
goal: Make a heavy thought visually smaller without arguing with its words.
steps:
1. Project — Project the sentence on an inner screen.
2. Shrink — Shrink it to caption size.
3. Move Metres — Move it two metres away.
4. Lower Opacity — Lower opacity, swap the heavy typeface for something ordinary, and place generous blank space around it.
5. Read Version — Read the edited version once, then look at real text nearby.
win: The sentence took up less imagined space, and your eyes returned to real text nearby.
supports:
• Look for one missing fact; ask what else could fit.
• Check the whole situation; add the missing context.
• Check another angle; ask what would disprove it.
• Notice absolute words like always; delay the verdict.
• Use a real example; check the base rate.
formula_flow: Project → Shrink → Move Metres → Lower Opacity → Read Version
safety:
PAUSE
Return to external grounding if visual manipulation feels unreal or disorienting.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: COMMAND DOWNGRADE
goal: Turn an inner command into information you can choose around.
steps:
1. Picture Command — Hear the command exactly as it arrives: ‘Leave now,’ ‘Check again,’ ‘You must reply.’
2. Downgrade It — Remove the command tone and turn it into an observation: ‘An urge to leave is here,’ ‘An urge to check is here,’ or ‘An urge to reply is here.’
3. Reject Authority — Let the urge give you information without giving it authority.
win: 'Must' became an urge you could notice without automatically carrying it out.
supports:
• Leave the trigger; make access harder.
• Remember urges peak and fall; delay ten minutes.
• Make access less convenient; avoid bargaining.
• Tell someone early; use your hands.
• Avoid bargaining with the urge; change locations.
formula_flow: Picture Command → Downgrade It → Reject Authority
safety:
PAUSE
Act immediately when the original command reflects genuine safety needs.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PASSENGER THOUGHT
goal: Complete one meaningful action while the unwanted thought rides along.
steps:
1. Choose Time — Choose one two-minute action that matters.
2. Ride Passenger — Invite the thought to ride in the passenger seat—audible, uncomfortable, unedited.
3. Keep Hands — Hold hands on the action wheel and complete the movement while it talks.
4. Who Drove? — At the destination, notice who actually drove.
win: The two-minute action finished even though the thought never had to disappear.
supports:
• Do the easiest useful part; remove one barrier.
• Make it visible; remove one obvious distraction.
• Start with one minute; open only what you need.
• Prepare the task in advance; shrink the first action.
• Lower standards briefly; use two minutes.
formula_flow: Choose Time → Ride Passenger → Keep Hands → Who Drove?
safety:
PAUSE
Shorten the trip if functioning or situational awareness drops.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RIDE THE CRAVING GRAPH
goal: Watch a craving as a changing curve before deciding what protects the next hour.
steps:
1. Level — Notice its current level and where it moves in the body.
2. Watch Slope — Watch for slope: rising, flattening, cresting, falling.
3. Imagine Urge — Every thirty seconds, imagine the next point without acting on the urge.
4. Name Change — When the line changes direction, name the change.
5. Choose Time — Choose what protects the next hour.
win: You noticed the urge's slope change without acting at its peak.
supports:
• Change rooms if possible; avoid bargaining.
• Delay ten minutes; do one incompatible activity.
• Delay acting for ten minutes; use your hands.
• Keep your hands busy; move away from the cue.
• Leave the trigger; avoid bargaining with the urge.
formula_flow: Level → Watch Slope → Imagine Urge → Name Change → Choose Time
safety:
PAUSE
Cravings linked to withdrawal, overdose, or medical danger require professional help.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PAIN PLUS THE FIGHT
goal: Separate the pain itself from the extra fight you are adding.
steps:
1. Make Two Lanes — Imagine two lanes: WHAT HURTS and WHAT RESISTANCE ADDS.
2. Keep The Hurt — In the first lane, picture the raw sensation or fact.
3. Catch The Fight — In the second lane, name demands, self-attack, bracing, and impossible arguments with reality.
4. Drop One Fight — Release one item from the resistance lane while respecting the hurt.
win: One layer of self-attack, bracing, or impossible demand was dropped while the hurt remained respected.
supports:
• Prefer repair; separate guilt from responsibility.
• Name the exact mistake; drop self-punishment.
• Use the same standard for everyone; name the mistake.
• Recall capability; name what was outside your control.
• Use equal standards; choose one repair.
formula_flow: Make Two Lanes → Keep The Hurt → Catch The Fight → Drop One Fight
safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CLOSE ONE DOOR FOR THIRTY SECONDS
goal: Test each leading option briefly to learn from your reaction without committing.
steps:
1. Close Door — Picture the two leading options. Mentally fade one for thirty seconds and pretend it is unavailable; do not commit.
2. Read Protest — Notice the first specific reaction—relief, disappointment, bargaining, urgency, or no change. Name it in four words or fewer.
3. Reopen Choice — Bring that option back. Repeat once with the other option faded so both reactions receive the same test.
4. Choose Next — Use the clearer reaction as one piece of data, then choose only the next responsible move.
win: Each option was removed and restored once, giving you new data for the next responsible move.
supports:
• Name the non-negotiables; limit the options.
• Reduce the options; ignore imagined regret.
• Use strongest evidence; commit once chosen.
• Stop researching after enough evidence; set a decision deadline.
• Accept one trade-off; choose by the strongest evidence.
formula_flow: Close Door → Read Protest → Reopen Choice → Choose Next
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use pretend closure for urgent, coercive, unsafe, or irreversible choices.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

ritual_name: CLOSE ONE DOOR FOR THIRTY SECONDS
ritualText:
CLOSE ONE DOOR FOR THIRTY SECONDS

PLAY TIME
about 90 seconds

GOAL
Test each leading option briefly to learn from your reaction without committing.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Close Door — Picture the two leading options. Mentally fade one for thirty seconds and pretend it is unavailable; do not commit.
2. Read Protest — Notice the first specific reaction—relief, disappointment, bargaining, urgency, or no change. Name it in four words or fewer.
3. Reopen Choice — Bring that option back. Repeat once with the other option faded so both reactions receive the same test.
4. Choose Next — Use the clearer reaction as one piece of data, then choose only the next responsible move.

WIN
Each option was removed and restored once, giving you new data for the next responsible move.

• Name the non-negotiables; limit the options.
• Reduce the options; ignore imagined regret.
• Use strongest evidence; commit once chosen.
• Stop researching after enough evidence; set a decision deadline.
• Accept one trade-off; choose by the strongest evidence.

MIND BEND
Relief or disappointment after a temporary loss can reveal preference without pretending emotion is a final verdict.

FORMULA FLOW
Close Door → Read Protest → Reopen Choice → Choose Next

SAFETY
PAUSE
Do not use pretend closure for urgent, coercive, unsafe, or irreversible choices.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: VALUE BEFORE CERTAINTY
goal: Let a chosen quality guide the next move before certainty arrives.
steps:
1. Ask Quality — Ask, “What quality should the next action carry?” Choose honesty, courage, care, fairness, or patience.
2. Make It Visible — Define one visible movement that expresses that quality today.
3. Let Certainty Wait — Let certainty remain absent while the chosen quality gives direction.
win: One visible action expressed the value you picked even though doubt was still present.
supports:
• Accept the trade-off; make the next hour reflect it.
• Remove one conflicting commitment; name what matters today.
• Keep meaning practical; pick one value for this decision.
• Check whose goal; protect important time.
• Choose aligned action; check whose goal you are chasing.

title: THE CONTROL GRAVEYARD
goal: Notice which control habits charge more over time than they repay now.
steps:
1. Use Control — Name everything used to control the feeling: checking, avoiding, numbing, arguing, extra certainty, overworking.
2. Picture Short — Beside each, picture the short-term payoff and the six-month bill.
3. Focus On Costs — Focus on any method whose bill exceeds its relief.
4. Choose Experiment — Choose one experiment in not paying that cost today.
win: You identified one short-term relief strategy whose longer bill was too high and skipped it once.
supports:
• Stop reopening choices; set a limit on checking.
• Name what is known; delay reassurance seeking.
• Accept small risk; notice when checking stops helping.
• Choose good enough; ask what is controllable now.
• Avoid reopening settled choices; choose a good-enough option.

PAUSE

title: THE SKY DOES NOT BECOME THE WEATHER
goal: Notice thoughts, feelings, and roles without shrinking yourself to any of them.
steps:
1. Name Thought — Name one thought, one feeling, and one role active now.
2. Say Being — For each, say: ‘This is being noticed.’ Search for the noticing itself—its colour, age, or mood.
3. Rest Openness — If none can be found, rest with that openness for ten seconds.
4. Land in Feet — Return by feeling both feet.
win: Each experience became something being noticed rather than the whole person noticing it.
supports:
• Choose one value-led action; act before motivation.
• Choose aligned action; check whose goal.
• Review what the action costs; remove one conflicting commitment.
• Name what matters today; review the cost.
• Pick one value for this decision; use one priority.
formula_flow: Name Thought → Say Being → Rest Openness → Land in Feet
safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN WITHOUT A TRIAL
goal: Return to what matters without turning a detour into a character trial.
steps:
1. State Off — State what moved off course in plain language.
2. Delete Adjectives — Remove every adjective about your character.
3. Name Value — Name the value still available, then take the smallest move that serves it now.
4. Check After — Only after moving, decide whether the plan itself needs repair.
5. Skip Verdict — Re-enter the plan without putting yourself on trial.
win: One value-based move happened before you judged yourself or redesigned the whole plan.
supports:
• Use one priority; choose aligned action.
• Act before motivation; choose one value-led action.
• Use values to choose trade-offs; keep meaning practical.
• Remove one conflict; review what the action costs.
• Accept the trade-off; check whose goal you are chasing.

safety:

title: THE THIRD VOICE
goal: Build a response that respects both the feeling and the verified facts.
steps:
1. Open Voices — Complete three lines.
2. Name Feeling — FEELING SAYS: include its full truth.
3. Name Facts — FACTS SAY: include only verified information.
4. Build Wisdom — WISE RESPONSE: honour the need in the first line and the constraints in the second.
5. Use Wisdom — Read only the third line before acting.
win: Your final response included the emotion's need without letting it overwrite reality.
supports:
• Use plain language; check the facts separately.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; let intensity fall.
• Delay the message; check basic needs.
• Name the feeling plainly; slow physical pace.
• Name the emotion; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
formula_flow: Open Voices → Name Feeling → Name Facts → Build Wisdom → Use Wisdom
safety:
PAUSE
Delay major action if either witness is too impaired to give usable information.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CAMERA FIRST, CAPTION SECOND
goal: Separate what a camera could record from the meaning you add afterward.
steps:
1. Camera Mode — For fifteen seconds, collect camera data: colour, movement, sound, pressure, position.
2. Describe Event — Then say the event using only that footage.
3. Add Caption — Now add the meaning separately and label it CAPTION.
4. Keep Sources — Keep both; never confuse their sources.
win: The event and your caption about it stayed in two different mental boxes.
supports:
• Make the new habit easier; notice the first automatic moment.
• Move the cue; reset without self-criticism.
• Keep replacement easy; change the environment.
• Change one cue; replace one response.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; reduce easy access to triggers.

safety:

title: TRANSLATE THE VERDICT
goal: Break a harsh judgment into facts, preference, and likely consequence.
steps:
1. Take Judgement — Take one judgement and mentally translate it into three components: visible facts, personal preference, likely consequence.
2. Prefer Decision — Example: ‘Awful meeting’ becomes ‘Two interruptions; I prefer turn-taking; the decision stayed unclear.’ Respond to the components rather than fighting the label.
win: The label stopped being one solid verdict and became separate pieces you could respond to.
supports:
• Interrupt the usual sequence; keep replacement easy.
• Interrupt the sequence; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Make the old habit harder; reset without self-criticism.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; move the cue.
• Change the environment; add small friction.

title: OBJECTIVE OVER EGO
goal: Choose the action that serves the real objective instead of protecting ego.
steps:

2. Name — Name the action that advances it and the action that merely wins, punishes, impresses, or avoids embarrassment.
3. Imagine Tomorrow — Imagine tomorrow’s result after each.
4. Select Works — Select what works, even if the ego receives no trophy.
win: The next move advanced the outcome even though it offered no trophy for winning or impressing.
supports:
• Use a visible cue; lower standards briefly.
• Open only what you need; stop planning after one action.
• Lower the first demand; skip extra setup.
• Start smaller; remove one barrier.
• Start before you feel ready; set a two-minute timer.

safety:
PAUSE

title: THE ATTENTION BOUNCER
goal: Decide which thought deserves attention instead of letting every thought enter.
steps:
1. Spot Arrival — Notice the next thought without following it.
2. Stamp Access — Stamp it REQUESTED, RELEVANT, or UNINVITED.
3. Set Budget — Give the chosen category five slow counts; let the others wait without argument.
4. Return Door — After five counts, return to the task or deliberately admit one new thought.
win: One thought received deliberate attention while the rest waited without a fight.
supports:
• Silence nonessential notifications; use one window at a time.
• Finish or park one open loop; return to one target.
• Mute alerts; choose one target.
• Close what you do not need; protect one focus block.
• Reduce nearby noise; keep one task visible.

PAUSE

title: ONE CLEAN WISH
goal: Hold compassion and a real boundary at the same time.
steps:
1. Bring Person — Bring the person to mind at a safe distance.
2. Keep It Honest — Choose one honest wish that does not deny harm: ‘May we both be free from causing more suffering,’ or ‘May safety become possible.’ Offer it once.
3. State Boundary — Then state the boundary or action you still need.
4. Keep Discernment — Warmth does not cancel discernment.
win: You offered one honest wish without weakening the boundary or action still needed.
supports:
• Delay your answer; protect your capacity.
• Leave their reaction with them; notice resentment early.
• Use one clear sentence; keep consequences realistic.
• Keep the limit simple; offer only genuine options.
• Leave reactions with them; use a short no.

title: THE 2% SOFTENING
goal: Test whether a tiny believable softening changes the body's defensive setting.
steps:
1. Release Forehead — Without forcing happiness, release the forehead, loosen the eyes, and lift the mouth corners by two percent.
2. Keep Expression — Keep the expression believable.
3. Hold Neutral — Hold it while resting your gaze on one neutral visual point.
4. Ask Whether — Ask whether defence changed by even half a notch.
win: One facial area eased slightly and you noticed whether defence shifted at all.
supports:
• Sip water if it helps; keep your body supported.
• Give the surge time to pass; reduce caffeine.
• Reduce extra stimulation; avoid symptom searching.
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; use ordinary surroundings.
• Keep movements gentle; loosen your shoulders.

safety:
PAUSE
Skip this if smiling feels unsafe, invalidating, painful, or socially risky.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PLAY THE BODY PASSWORD
goal: Use a slow movement sequence to prove your body can follow deliberate instructions.
steps:
1. Set Code — Choose three tiny comfortable movements, such as tap a knee, touch a thumb, and shift your gaze.
2. Run Order — Do A–B–C slowly, pausing after each movement long enough to feel it finish.
3. Reverse Code — Do C–B–A at the same pace. If you lose the order, restart instead of speeding up.
4. Claim Control — Name the movement you directed most clearly, then let the code stop.
win: You completed the pattern forward and backward without speeding through a mistake.
supports:
• Sip water if it helps; wait out the surge.
• Keep your body supported; unclench your jaw.
• Reduce extra stimulation; let breathing stay natural.
• Give the surge time to pass; let breaths happen.
• Loosen your shoulders; look at ordinary objects nearby.
formula_flow: Set Code → Run Order → Reverse Code → Claim Control
safety:
PAUSE
Do not play while driving, moving through hazards, dizzy, injured, or unable to stay oriented.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

goal: Use brief comfortable coolness as a reset cue, not a toughness test.
steps:

win: The cool sensation landed, you re-oriented to the room, and chose the next safe action.
supports:

• Let breaths happen; avoid repeated pulse checking.

title: THE LONGER OUT-BREATH
goal: Lengthen the out-breath gently, then make one workable decision from a steadier pace.
steps:
1. Breathe Pulling — Breathe in without pulling extra air.
2. Let Outflow — Let the outflow last slightly longer, as though fogging a distant window silently.
3. Repeat Comfortable — Repeat only while comfortable; keep shoulders quiet and jaw loose.
4. Breathe Workable — After several rounds, resume natural breathing and look for one workable decision.
win: Breathing returned to normal and one next decision looked usable rather than urgent.
supports:
• Accept one trade-off; stop extra research.
• Use strongest evidence; name the non-negotiables.
• Name must-haves; reduce the options.
• Set a deadline; ask what failure would cost.
• Commit once chosen; set a decision deadline.

safety:
PAUSE
Return to ordinary breathing immediately if light-headed, air-hungry, or panicky.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIVE SAFE SIGNALS
goal: Receive five ordinary sensory cues slowly enough for one to feel trustworthy.
steps:
1. Build Sensory — Build a sensory sequence from what is available: one pleasing sight, steady sound, comforting texture, mild scent, and nourishing taste.
2. Receive Instead — Spend a few seconds receiving each instead of rushing to the next cue.
3. End Sense — End on the sense that feels most trustworthy today.
win: You reached the final sense without rushing and knew which cue felt most steady today.
supports:
• Accept one trade-off; avoid reopening without new facts.
• Keep new facts separate; name must-haves.
• Name the non-negotiables; stop researching after enough evidence.
• Choose by the strongest evidence; pick the reversible option first.
• Choose reversible first; set a decision deadline.

title: DROP THE APPEAL
goal: Stop arguing with the existence of what happened and respond to the reality that remains.
steps:
1. State Fact — State the fact in plain past or present tense.
2. Remove Approval — Remove approval, blame, and every “should not have happened.” Notice the body’s protest and answer: “Not liking it is allowed; refusing its existence adds nothing.”
3. Add Nothing — Choose the next response available in the world that actually exists.
win: The fact stayed plain, the 'shouldn't' was removed, and one real-world response became available.
supports:
• Ask for a specific next action; lead with the point.
• Separate tone from facts; name the desired change.
• Confirm who will do what; check the request.
• End with action; confirm the owner.
• Clarify the deadline; ask what they heard.
formula_flow: State Fact → Remove Approval → Add Nothing
safety:
PAUSE
Acceptance must never be used to legitimise abuse, injustice, or preventable harm.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DOES THE FEELING FIT THE FILE?
goal: Check whether the feeling's intensity matches the verified present threat.
steps:
1. Imagine Four Lanes — Picture four lanes: event, meaning, verified evidence, present threat.
2. Compare Emotion — Compare the emotion’s intensity with the present-threat lane.
3. Use Feeling — If they fit, use the feeling’s message.
4. Update Meaning — If they exceed it, regulate first and revise the meaning.
win: You either used the emotion's message or regulated first because the facts did not support its volume.
supports:
• Use plain language; do one steadying action.
• Slow physical pace; check basic needs.
• Name the feeling plainly; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Check the facts separately; use simple words for the problem.
• Separate feeling from fact; lower stimulation for a minute.
formula_flow: Imagine Four Lanes → Compare Emotion → Use Feeling → Update Meaning
safety:
PAUSE
Trust immediate protective action when evidence shows real threat.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: REVERSE THE URGE, COMPLETELY
goal: When the facts allow it, give an unhelpful urge a full safe opposite signal.
steps:
1. Check Support — Verify that the facts do not support the action impulse.
2. Speak Gently — Then do its full safe opposite: approach instead of avoid, speak gently instead of attack, straighten instead of collapse, engage instead of hide.
3. Match Posture — Match posture, words, and behaviour until the new signal is coherent.
win: Posture, words, and behaviour all pointed away from the original impulse.
supports:
• Drink some water; avoid bargaining.
• Change locations; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Make access less convenient; eat if hungry.
• Make access harder; keep your hands busy.
• Avoid bargaining with the urge; ride the peak.
formula_flow: Check Support → Speak Gently → Match Posture
safety:
PAUSE
Never oppose an urge that correctly protects you from danger or violation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FEELING OR FIXING?
goal: Decide whether the remaining problem needs soothing, action, or support.
steps:
1. Drop Define — After body alarm drops, define the obstacle without emotional adjectives.
2. Ask Whether — Ask if one specific action could change it.
3. Choose Action — If yes, choose and schedule that action.
4. Return Acceptance — If no, return to acceptance or support.
5. Stop Soothing — Do not keep using soothing when the door requires a key.
win: After the body settled, you could tell whether there was a practical door that needed a key.
supports:
• Avoid symptom searching; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Unclench your jaw; let breaths happen.
• Use ordinary surroundings; let breathing stay natural.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; stop body scanning.
• Reduce caffeine; keep your body supported.

title: LET THE EMOTION FINISH ONE CHAPTER
goal: Let the current emotional chapter finish before jumping into the next one.
steps:
1. Identify Chapter — Spot the current chapter only: sensation, meaning, action urge, or settling.
2. Permit — Permit the next natural chapter while withholding later ones.
3. Pause Meaning — If sensation is active, do not interpret; if meaning is clear, do not act yet.
4. Continue Genuine — Continue until a genuine settling marker—breath change, warmth, tears ending, posture release—appears.
win: A real settling marker appeared without sensation, meaning, and action being rushed together.
supports:
• Change locations; make access harder.
• Eat if hungry; ride the peak.
• Make access less convenient; avoid bargaining with the urge.
• Leave the trigger; change rooms if possible.
• Tell someone early; avoid bargaining.
formula_flow: Identify Chapter → Permit → Pause Meaning → Continue Genuine
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if the process floods awareness or removes action control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: STAY FOR THE UPDATE
goal: Stay with a manageable fear cue long enough to notice reality contradict one prediction.
steps:
1. Choose External — Choose an external cue low enough on your fear ladder to approach voluntarily.
2. Enter Escape — Enter without escape and remain until you observe at least one mismatch between prediction and reality.
3. Name Mismatch — Name the mismatch before leaving.
4. Repeat Later — Repeat later under safe conditions rather than chasing maximum distress.
win: You left after naming one mismatch between what you expected and what actually occurred.
supports:
• Reset after slips; change one cue.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; interrupt the sequence.
• Make the new habit easier; change the environment first.
• Change the environment; notice the trigger.
• Interrupt the usual sequence; notice the first automatic moment.

title: READ THE SIGNAL WITHOUT TURNING IT UP
goal: Describe one existing body sensation neutrally and stop after one sensible check.
steps:
1. Notice Existing Signal — Notice only a sensation already present and do not intensify it.
2. Check Outside Facts — Check the room, recent activity, and any known medical information.
3. Name Neutral Quality — Describe the sensation with neutral words such as warm, tight, or moving.
4. Choose Safe Response — Choose rest, ordinary movement, support, or medical advice as appropriate.
5. End The Check — Stop after one check and avoid repeated body monitoring.
win: The sensation was named without amplification, and the next response matched context rather than repeated monitoring.
supports:
• Sip water if it helps; keep movements gentle.
• Stop body scanning; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Give the surge time to pass; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Let breathing stay natural; reduce extra stimulation.
formula_flow: Notice Existing Signal → Check Outside Facts → Name Neutral Quality → Choose Safe Response → End The Check
safety:
PAUSE
Do not deliberately trigger, intensify, or test feared body sensations. Use this content only as non-exposure education unless a qualified clinician has assessed and supervised an exposure plan. Seek medical advice for uncertain symptoms.
This is not diagnosis, treatment, or emergency care.

title: LEAVE ONE QUESTION OPEN
goal: Leave one low-stakes question unanswered until a chosen review time.
steps:
1. Choose Low — Choose a low-stakes unknown.
2. Picture Card — Picture it on a card and forbid checking, asking, or mentally solving until a set time.
3. Carry Unanswered — Carry the unanswered card while doing normal life.
4. Watch The Urge — At review, notice what the urge did—not whether certainty arrived.
win: Normal life continued while the urge to solve or check changed on its own.
supports:
• Act with uncertainty; use a deadline.
• Notice when checking stops helping; name what is unknown.
• Name what is known; act on the safest workable option.
• Limit checking; accept a small margin of risk.
• Set a limit on checking; ask what is controllable now.

title: STAY THROUGH RECOVERY
goal: Remain with a safe practice cue through the first signs of recovery, then end deliberately.
steps:
1. Highest — During a safe practice round, notice the highest point and the first downward shift.
2. Stay Past Relief — Do not leave at that first relief.
3. Remain Cue — Remain with the cue through a visible recovery phase—steady gaze, slower movement, reduced urge—then end on purpose.
4. Leave After Recovery — Departure follows learning, not panic.
win: You stayed past the first relief until your gaze, movement, or urge showed visible recovery.
supports:
• Let breathing stay natural; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Wait out the surge; reduce caffeine.
• Avoid symptom searching; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Use ordinary surroundings; keep your body supported.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; loosen your shoulders.

title: REMOVE ONE INVISIBLE CRUTCH
goal: Drop one unnecessary safety habit while keeping real safety intact.
steps:
1. Identify Protective — During a manageable practice round, spot one protective act that is unnecessary: gripping, rehearsing, sitting by the exit, checking pulse, carrying extra certainty.
2. Drop Legitimate — Drop only that act while keeping legitimate safety intact.
3. Observe Outcome — Observe what the outcome says without it.
win: The practice continued without one protective crutch, giving you evidence about what happened in its absence.
supports:
• Lower standards briefly; reward starting, not finishing.
• Choose a rough beginning; restart quickly.
• Remove one barrier; set a two-minute timer.
• Use two minutes; begin with the easiest part.
• Lower the quality bar; start physically.

title: MOVE THE LESSON
goal: Carry a learned skill into changing conditions instead of trusting it only in one setting.
steps:
1. Repeat Mastered — Repeat a mastered practice while changing one feature: location, time, cue order, duration, or intensity.
2. Change Again — On the next round, alter a different feature.
3. Map Transfer — Keep a small mental map of where the skill still works.
4. Make Portable — Let variation turn a local success into portable knowledge.
win: The skill still worked after at least one feature of the context was deliberately changed.
supports:
• Ask what would disprove it; use current facts.
• Use a real example; question absolute words.
• Check the whole situation; delay the verdict.
• Check the base rate; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Separate possibility from probability; use recent, concrete evidence.

safety:

title: THE TWO-CUE MERGE
goal: Combine two manageable triggers and compare the real effect with what you predicted.
steps:
1. Select Triggers — Select two triggers already manageable separately.
2. Predict Joining — Predict what joining them will add.
3. Drop Unnecessary — Contact both at a modest dose while dropping unnecessary escape.
4. Stay Long — Stay long enough to compare the combined result with the prediction, then recover fully.
win: Both cues were present together long enough to reveal whether their combined impact matched the forecast.
supports:
• Reduce easy access to triggers; replace one response.
• Reset without self-criticism; change one cue.
• Make the old habit harder; change the environment first.
• Remove easy access; make the new habit easier.
• Add small friction; interrupt the usual sequence.

title: FINISH THE LOOK
goal: Let your eyes finish checking the present before deciding where attention belongs.
steps:
1. Let Eyes — Let your eyes move before your head.
2. Scan Left — Slowly scan left, centre, right, behind if safe, and toward an exit.
3. Name Cues — Name present cues of choice, support, and distance from threat.
4. Allow Neck — Allow the neck to follow only within comfort.
5. Place Attention — End by selecting where attention belongs now.
win: Choice, support, distance, and an exit were all visually located without forcing the neck or returning to the past.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; wait before sending messages.
• Use plain language; notice body tension.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; notice what changed physically.
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; slow physical pace.
• Rest before deciding; use simple words for the problem.

PAUSE

title: PENDULUM BETWEEN TWO TRUTHS
goal: Move attention between activation and steadiness without getting trapped in either.
steps:
1. Find Activated — Find one activated region and another settled or supported area.
2. Move Resource — Touch the difficult region with attention for a few seconds, then move to the resource.
3. Travel — Travel back and forth at a pace that preserves choice.
4. Finish Whichever — Finish on whichever location offers steadier awareness of your location.
win: You travelled between a difficult area and a supported area while preserving choice about pace.
supports:
• Use ordinary surroundings; sip water if it helps.
• Sit somewhere safe; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Keep your body supported; give the surge time to pass.
• Unclench your jaw; loosen your shoulders.
• Keep movements gentle; wait out the surge.

title: ONE DROP, NOT THE OCEAN
goal: Touch only the smallest workable piece of difficult material and recover fully.
steps:
1. Choose Tiniest — Choose the tiniest fragment of the difficult material: one edge, colour, word, or body sensation.
2. Return Fully — Contact it briefly, then return fully to a stabilising cue.
3. Find Dose — Hold the dose that allowed recovery.
4. Use Less — Next practice uses the same or less—not an ambitious leap.
win: A tiny dose was contacted and left without needing a bigger challenge on the next round.
supports:
• Give the surge time to pass; sit somewhere safe.
• Reduce extra stimulation; stop body scanning.
• Keep movements gentle; let breaths happen.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Loosen your shoulders; keep your body supported.

title: TRACK WHAT HOLDS
goal: Strengthen one real body signal of steadiness instead of searching only for what feels wrong.
steps:
1. Locate Bodily — Locate one bodily sign of steadiness—warmth, pressure, uprightness, ease, or a capable impulse.
2. Describe Boundaries — Say its boundaries and changes for twenty seconds.
3. Ask Memory — Ask what memory, person, posture, or environment strengthens it by one degree.
4. Add Support — Add only that support.
win: A specific steady sensation was located, described, and supported by one thing that increased it slightly.
supports:
• Delay acting for ten minutes; do one incompatible activity.

title: WAIT FOR THE WHOLE BODY ANSWER
goal: Let the body give a whole-picture response before analysis takes over.
steps:
1. Bring Mind — Bring the issue to mind lightly, then pause verbal analysis.
2. Ask Body — Ask the body, ‘What is the whole of this like?’ Wait for an image, phrase, posture, or global texture.
3. Check Whether — Check whether it fits by noticing a small inner yes, no, or shift.
4. Leave It Raw — Leave the answer unpolished.
win: An image, phrase, posture, or felt texture arrived and was checked for a small inner fit.
supports:
• Avoid symptom searching; give the surge time to pass.
• Stop body scanning; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Reduce caffeine; let breaths happen.
• Keep movements gentle; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; use ordinary surroundings.

safety:
PAUSE
End the inquiry if bodily attention creates panic, numbness, or feeling unreal or disconnected.

title: COMPLETE THE DEFENCE IN MINIATURE
goal: Let a safe defensive impulse finish in miniature instead of freezing halfway.
steps:
1. Small — Notice the small impulse to push, turn, step back, shield, or say no.
2. Let Unfold — In a safe space, let it unfold slowly at ten percent strength.
3. Stop Completion — Stop at the natural completion and return to neutral posture.
4. Observe Whether — Observe whether the body receives an ending.
win: A tiny push, turn, step, shield, or no reached a natural endpoint and returned to neutral.
supports:
• Ride the peak; change locations.
• Make access harder; change rooms if possible.
• Use your hands; do one incompatible activity.
• Drink some water; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Move away from the cue; eat if hungry.
formula_flow: Small → Let Unfold → Stop Completion → Observe Whether
safety:
PAUSE
Never direct movement toward a person or continue if aggression escalates.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BORROW THE FLOOR
goal: Feel what the surface is already holding instead of trying to manufacture grounding.
steps:
1. Choose Contact — Choose one contact point—feet, seat, back, forearms, or hands.
2. Release Extra — Increase pressure slightly, then release extra effort and notice what the surface continues to carry.
3. Name Texture — Name its texture, temperature, and steadiness.
4. Trust Ground — You need not manufacture a sense of ground.
win: Pressure softened while texture, temperature, and steadiness remained available through one contact point.
supports:
• Keep eyes open; notice temperature and texture.
• Reduce sensory input if needed; feel your feet.
• Look around slowly; notice where your body is supported.
• Feel both feet; name today's date.
• Notice room temperature; feel the chair.

safety:

title: CATCH THE RECOVERY SIGNAL
goal: Notice the first real sign that body alarm is already beginning to recover.
steps:
1. Watch Swallow — After body alarm, watch for a swallow, sigh, warmth, trembling, yawn, moisture in the eyes, breath shift, or muscle release.
2. Name Accurately — When one appears, name it accurately and stay with its after-effect.
3. No Extra Trigger — Do not provoke more.
4. Look Like — Teach the mind what recovery looks like.
win: A swallow, sigh, warmth, tremble, yawn, tear, breath shift, or muscle release was recognised without provoking more.
supports:
• Sit somewhere safe; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Loosen your shoulders; give the surge time to pass.
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; wait out the surge.
• Let breathing stay natural; keep movements gentle.
• Unclench your jaw; look at ordinary objects nearby.
formula_flow: Watch Swallow → Name Accurately → No Extra Trigger → Look Like
safety:
PAUSE
Seek care if shaking, breathing changes, or other symptoms seem medically concerning.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DATE-STAMP THE PRESENT
goal: Anchor to today's date using the room, an exit, and reachable support.
steps:
1. Name Today's Date — Say today's full date and your current location aloud.
2. Read Three Objects — Read the names of three ordinary objects directly in front of you.
3. Locate Current Exit — Point to the nearest safe exit without moving toward the past memory.
4. Name Available Support — Name one person or service available in the present.
5. Return To Room — Keep eyes open and return attention to the whole room.
win: Today's date, current location, ordinary objects, a safe exit, and a present-day helper all became explicit.
supports:
• Stop if less present; choose gentle, ordinary movement.
• Orient to today's date and place; avoid forcing detailed memories.
• Contact someone you trust; move gently.
• Stop if you feel less present; hold a familiar object.
• Name the place; contact someone trusted.
formula_flow: Name Today's Date → Read Three Objects → Locate Current Exit → Name Available Support → Return To Room
safety:
PAUSE
Keep your eyes open. Use only present-day room, date, place and support orientation. Do not revisit memories in detail, use trauma imagery, intensify sensations, or attempt unsupervised processing. Stop for flooding, dissociation, or weakened orientation and connect with qualified human support.
This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

title: ONE FOOT HERE, EYES OPEN
goal: Re-anchor in the current room without pulling more detail from the past.
steps:

title: SET THE CONVERSATION SIZE
goal: Fit the conversation to the amount you can safely handle right now.
steps:
1. Read Bandwidth — Choose your current safe bandwidth: ONE SENTENCE, THREE SENTENCES, or FULL CONVERSATION.
2. Choose Size — Name the purpose that must fit inside that size: acknowledge, request, pause, clarify, or repair.
3. Send Signal — Draft or say only the selected amount. Stop when the sentence limit is reached, even if more remains.
4. Set Reopen — Name when or under what condition the next level can reopen. If you cannot offer one, state that honestly without making a false promise.
win: You stopped at the chosen sentence limit and made the condition for reopening clear.
supports:
• Lead with the point; end with action.
• Separate facts from tone; check the request.
• Use shorter sentences when tense; keep one issue.
• Separate tone from facts; keep one issue per conversation.
• Check the agreed deadline; avoid guessing their intent.

PLAY TIME
60–90 seconds

GOAL
Notice early loss of steadiness and know exactly when self-help should stop.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Name Early Change — Name one early sign that present-time steadiness is weakening.
2. Choose External Grounding — Choose an eyes-open external grounding action that usually remains safe.
3. Set Stop Threshold — Set the point where all self-help must stop.
4. Pick Support Route — Choose the support route you will use and make it easy to find.
5. Share The Plan — Share the short plan with someone trustworthy before it is needed.

WIN
You had a grounding action, a stop point, and a support route ready before the alarm became stronger.

• Contact someone trusted; stop if you feel less present.
• Contact someone you trust; orient to today's date and place.
• Hold something familiar; choose gentle, ordinary movement.
• Keep your eyes open if safer; name today's date.
• Keep lighting comfortable; use familiar surroundings.

MIND BEND
A safety plan works best before judgment narrows. Deciding the handoff point early protects choice later.

Name Early Change → Choose External Grounding → Set Stop Threshold → Pick Support Route → Share The Plan

PAUSE

This is stabilisation only, not trauma treatment.

title: STAMP WHERE THE DETAIL CAME FROM
goal: Rate a memory detail by where it came from, not by how intense it feels.
steps:
1. Pick Detail — Choose one small memory detail; do not mentally revisit the event in detail.
2. Tag Source — Stamp it SENSED, INFERRED, LEARNED LATER, or UNSURE.
3. Rate Confidence — Give the detail a confidence word—high, medium, low, or unknown—based on its source rather than its emotional intensity.
4. Keep Core — Picture one core fact that remains reliable and let the other detail keep its honest uncertainty.
win: The detail received a source label and honest confidence while one reliable core fact stayed separate.
supports:
• Name what is unknown; notice when checking stops helping.
• Use a deadline; delay reassurance.
• Limit checking; name what is known.
• Accept a small margin of risk; leave one question unanswered.
• Stop reopening choices; use a decision deadline.
formula_flow: Pick Detail → Tag Source → Rate Confidence → Keep Core
safety:
PAUSE
Do not force missing details; stop and seek support if the memory becomes overwhelming or disorienting.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET BREATH BREATHE YOU
goal: Let breathing happen by itself while you simply notice its movement.
steps:
1. Follow Breaths — Follow three natural breaths exactly as they occur.
2. Leave Breath Alone — Do not deepen, slow, count, or improve them.
3. Start — Notice where each begins by itself and where it ends without instruction.
4. Let Body — Between breaths, let the body choose again.
5. Witness Motion — Your only action is witnessing what already knows how to move.
win: Three breaths began and ended without being corrected, deepened, slowed, or counted.
supports:
• Reduce commentary; return to the room.
• Use fewer words; notice where attention goes.
• Drop the need to solve it; notice the thought.
• Do not debate every detail; avoid building a larger story.
• Use simple present-tense facts; notice the thought, then step back.
formula_flow: Follow Breaths → Leave Breath Alone → Start → Let Body → Witness Motion
safety:
PAUSE
Use outward sensory contact if breath attention increases panic or air hunger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIND THE BUSY HALF
goal: Find which half of breathing is working too hard and ease only that side.
steps:
1. Observe Ordinary — Observe three ordinary cycles.
2. Rate Inhale — Rate inhale effort and exhale release separately.
3. Phase — Which phase is working too hard.
4. Leave Timing — Ease only that side toward neutral—less pulling in or less pushing out—while leaving timing alone.
5. Check Whether — Check if urgency changes when imbalance decreases.
win: Inhale and exhale effort were compared separately, and only the busier phase moved toward neutral.
supports:
• Keep context visible; choose your own measure.
• Notice hidden differences; compare with your past self.
• Name one thing already working; avoid one-person benchmarks.
• Stop checking their numbers; return to your own baseline.
• Notice what you cannot see; use your own timeline.
formula_flow: Observe Ordinary → Rate Inhale → Phase → Leave Timing → Check Whether
safety:
PAUSE
Stop adjustment at the first sign of dizziness, strain, or breath fixation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE EVEN BRIDGE
goal: Balance inhale and exhale gently, then let counting disappear.
steps:

supports:

• Stay somewhere physically safe; reduce extra stimulation.
• Keep your body supported; let breaths happen.
• Let breathing stay natural; loosen your shoulders.
• Wait out the surge; unclench your jaw and shoulders.

title: ALTERNATE THE AIRWAY
goal: Alternate nostrils gently without holding, forcing, or chasing a special state.
steps:
1. Sit Easy — Sit comfortably.
2. Close Nostril — Without force, close one nostril and breathe through the other; switch sides for the next gentle cycle.
3. Continue Unhurried — Continue alternating with an unhurried hand.
4. Keep Breath — Keep the breath quiet and abandon retention.
5. Open Both Sides — Finish with both sides open and let breathing return to normal.
win: Both sides were used quietly and the practice ended with normal breathing restored.
supports:
• Delay the message; name the emotion.
• Slow physical pace; use simple words for the problem.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; check the facts separately.
• Rest before deciding; avoid decisions at peak emotion.
• Name the feeling plainly; lower nearby noise.

title: OCEAN IN THE THROAT
goal: Make the breath softly audible, then soften effort until the sound nearly disappears.
steps:
1. Create Soft — Narrow the throat only enough to create a soft ocean texture, never a rasp.

4. Release Technique — After several waves, release the technique completely.

title: EXHALE IN CHAPTERS
goal: Let the exhale leave in soft sections, then wait for the next inhale.
steps:
1. Let Air — Instead of one continuous out-breath, let air leave in three soft portions with tiny unforced spaces between.
2. Keep Face — Keep the face loose and never push to empty.
3. Wait Body — After the final segment, wait for the body’s next inhale rather than grabbing it.
win: Three gentle portions finished without pushing empty, and the body supplied the next breath on its own.
supports:
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; stop body scanning.
• Let breaths happen; keep your body supported.
• Reduce caffeine; avoid symptom searching.
• Loosen your shoulders; sip water if it helps.
• Use ordinary surroundings; wait out the surge.
formula_flow: Let Air → Keep Face → Wait Body
safety:
PAUSE
Resume normal breathing if segmentation causes urgency or tingling.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE RETURN REP
goal: Count honest returns of attention instead of demanding unbroken focus.
steps:
1. Select Neutral — Select one neutral anchor.
2. Attention — Each time distraction appears, notice where attention went and escort it back without commentary.
3. Count Rather — Count returns rather than uninterrupted seconds.
4. End After — Finish after ten honest comebacks, even if focus never felt perfect.
win: Ten distractions became ten successful comebacks rather than ten failures.
supports:
• Set finish time; ask what is actually required.
• Define good enough first; compare against the brief.
• Ship the useful part; separate errors from polish.
• Define good enough; leave minor flaws alone.
• Make the rough version first; stop low-value changes.

about 1 minute

GOAL

title: NO FAVOURITE SENSATION
goal: Give pleasant, unpleasant, dull, and vivid sensations the same brief welcome.
steps:
1. Let Field — Let the field choose its next foreground.
2. Pleasant — Pleasant, unpleasant, dull, or vivid—offer each the same brief hospitality.
3. Include Movement — When preference reaches to grip or reject, include that movement too.
4. End Whole — End by noticing the whole room at once.
win: Preference itself became another event in the field instead of deciding what had to stay or leave.
supports:
• Notice the first automatic moment; remove easy access.
• Replace one response; interrupt the sequence.
• Move the cue; reset after slips.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; make the old habit harder.
• Notice the trigger; delay the routine.
formula_flow: Let Field → Pleasant → Include Movement → End Whole
safety:
PAUSE
Use a stable anchor instead during high body alarm or feeling unreal or disconnected.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

win: A single word named the event without turning into an explanation about it.

• Avoid treating guesses as facts; check what you actually know.
• Check another angle; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Check the base rate; use current facts.

title: THE SENSE ROLL CALL
goal: Reconnect with the room through a precise five-sense inventory.
steps:
1. Find Five — Find five distinct colours or shapes, four contact sensations, three separate sounds, two scents, and one taste or mouth sensation.
2. Answer Blue — No generic answers; ‘blue attention’ beats ‘something blue.’ Let the inventory end with the most stable item.
win: Specific colours, contacts, sounds, scents, and mouth sensation led you to one especially stable cue.
supports:
• Keep eyes open; feel both feet.
• Notice three colours; name today's date.
• Track one texture; notice where your body is supported.
• Touch a stable surface; notice room temperature.
• Hear one real sound; feel your feet.
formula_flow: Find Five → Answer Blue
safety:
PAUSE
Adapt counts or omit channels that are unavailable or triggering.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

2. Answer Blue — No generic answers; ‘blue attention’ beats ‘something blue.’ Let the inventory end with the most stable item.

Specific colours, contacts, sounds, scents, and mouth sensation led you to one especially stable cue.

• Keep eyes open; feel both feet.
• Notice three colours; name today's date.
• Track one texture; notice where your body is supported.
• Touch a stable surface; notice room temperature.
• Hear one real sound; feel your feet.

Grounding becomes stronger when perception is specific; 'something blue' asks less of attention than actually seeing which blue thing is here.

PAUSE

title: RAIN WITHOUT THE UMBRELLA
goal: Acknowledge what is here, meet it kindly, and remember it is not all of you.
steps:
1. Recognise — Recognise what is here.
2. Allow Moment — Allow this moment of it to exist.
3. Question About — Investigate with one kind question about body or need.
4. Experience — Notice that the experience is present but not the whole of you.
5. Move R — Move through R–A–I–N once; resolution is not a required fifth letter.
win: The experience was recognised, allowed, gently investigated, and placed inside a larger sense of self.
supports:
• Do one steadying action; separate feeling from fact.
• Wait before sending messages; name the emotion.
• Use simple words for the problem; slow physical pace.
• Notice what changed physically; delay the message.
• Rest before deciding; use plain language.

safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FOUR PARTS OF ONE STEP
goal: Walk slowly enough to notice the four physical parts of each step.
steps:
1. Place Weight — Slow enough to separate lift, travel, place, and weight transfer.
2. Follow Events — Follow those four events through several steps.
3. Thought — When thought pulls away, rejoin at whichever phase the foot is currently performing.
4. Finish Walking — Finish by walking normally while retaining one point of contact.
win: Attention rejoined the foot at its current phase whenever thought pulled away.
supports:
• Take a short break; return to one target.
• Return after interruptions; park secondary tasks.
• Put the phone out of reach; reduce background noise.
• Close extra tabs; protect one focus block.
• Use one screen; clear visual clutter.
formula_flow: Place Weight → Follow Events → Thought → Finish Walking
safety:
PAUSE
Practise only where slowed walking is physically safe.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LISTEN PAST THE SOUND
goal: Follow a sound all the way into silence without replaying it in memory.
steps:
1. Play Safe — Ring, play, or notice a safe sustained sound.
2. Follow Decay — Follow its decay with precision until you cannot locate any remainder.
3. Stay Silence — Stay with the silence that receives it, not with memory of the tone.
4. Let Surroundings — Let the next surroundings sound end the practice.
win: The tone disappeared completely and the next real sound, not the remembered one, ended the practice.
supports:
• Reset after slips; move the cue.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Notice the first automatic moment; make the new habit easier.
• Remove easy access; change the environment first.
• Keep replacement easy; interrupt the sequence.
formula_flow: Play Safe → Follow Decay → Stay Silence → Let Surroundings
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid intense volume or tones associated with distress.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE BREATH HINGE
goal: Feel the natural turning points of breathing without holding them open.
steps:
1. Follow Inhale — Follow a natural inhale to the instant it turns toward exhale.
2. Leave Hinge Free — Do not hold or stretch the hinge.
3. Change — Notice the same effortless change at the bottom of exhalation.
4. Allow Breaths — Visit each threshold lightly, then allow several breaths to pass unwatched.
win: Both breath hinges were noticed lightly and several later breaths were allowed to pass unwatched.
supports:
• Stop body scanning; use ordinary surroundings.
• Let breaths happen; loosen your shoulders.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Keep your body supported; sit somewhere safe.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; unclench your jaw and shoulders.

safety:
PAUSE
Leave the hinge alone if waiting creates retention or air hunger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHERE SOUND BECOMES HEARING
goal: Follow a sound toward the point where 'outside' becomes hearing.
steps:
1. Listen Sustained — Listen to a sustained, gentle sound.
2. Follow Apparent — Follow it from apparent distance toward the place where it becomes an auditory experience—ear, head, body, or nowhere locatable.
3. Rest Briefly — When the border between outside vibration and inside hearing blurs, rest there briefly.
win: The boundary between vibration out there and auditory experience in here became less definite for a moment.
supports:
• Wait before sending messages; do one steadying action.
• Let intensity fall; check the facts separately.
• Check basic needs; give the feeling time to move.
• Notice body tension; delay the message.
• Name the feeling plainly; use plain language.
formula_flow: Listen Sustained → Follow Apparent → Rest Briefly
safety:
PAUSE
Choose ordinary grounding if auditory focus feels intrusive or voice-like.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BORROW THE SKY’S WIDTH
goal: Widen your visual field enough to hold outer space and inner contraction together.
steps:
1. Open Sky — Gaze softly into open sky or another unobstructed safe field.
2. Release Pinpoint — Release pinpoint focus and include the edges of vision.
3. Compare Width — Without forcing calm, compare the width outside with the contraction inside.
4. Keep Wide View — Allow attention to occupy both.
win: Peripheral vision opened while the tightness inside remained allowed rather than forced away.
supports:
• Return after interruptions; silence nonessential notifications.
• Take a real screen break; keep one task visible.
• Put the phone out of reach; return to one target.
• Clear visual clutter; close extra tabs.
• Finish or park one open loop; use one screen.
formula_flow: Open Sky → Release Pinpoint → Compare Width → Keep Wide View
safety:
PAUSE
Never sky-gaze while driving or in unsafe light and weather.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET DARKNESS BE COMPLETE
goal: Look at darkness as a visual field without filling it with imagined shapes.
steps:
1. Set Darkness — In a safe darkened setting, notice darkness as the actual visual field.
2. Return Unfilled — When the mind manufactures shapes or stories, recognise image production and return to the unfilled field.
3. Stay Briefly — Stay briefly, then reintroduce light on purpose.
win: Mental images were noticed as image-making, and the unfilled darkness became visible again.
supports:
• Keep one task visible; mute alerts.
• Close extra tabs; clear visual clutter.
• Return after interruptions; use one screen.
• Close what you do not need; park secondary tasks.
• Choose one target; put the phone out of reach.
formula_flow: Set Darkness → Return Unfilled → Stay Briefly
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid this practice if darkness triggers panic, trauma, or perceptual disturbance.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

steps:

win: The first pull was observed as movement before the desired thing was named or pursued.

• Reset without self-criticism; make the old habit harder.
• Replace one response; move the cue.
• Notice the first automatic moment; add small friction.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Change the environment; make the new habit easier.
