title: FEAR WITHOUT THE MOVIE
goal: Feel fear as raw body sensation without letting prediction turn it into a movie.
steps:
1. Locate Most — If safely steady, locate the most intense fear sensation and say only its movement, charge, heat, and boundary.
2. Remove Prediction — Remove prediction briefly.
3. Keep Hand — Keep one hand or gaze anchored in the room.
4. Let Raw — Let raw body alarm be observed without following its film script.
win: Heat, movement, charge, or boundary stayed observable while your hand or gaze remained anchored in the room.
supports:
• Reduce extra stimulation; sip water if it helps.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; sit somewhere safe.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; keep your body supported.
• Wait out the surge; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; loosen your shoulders.

safety:
PAUSE

title: WATCH PLEASURE LEAVE CLEANLY
goal: Let a pleasant sensation fade completely without immediately reaching for another dose.

win: Pleasure rose, thinned, and returned toward neutral while you resisted topping it up.

• Reset after slips; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Make the new habit easier; keep replacement easy.
• Notice the first automatic moment; change one cue.

title: FOLLOW IT TO ZERO
goal: Stay with one thought until it naturally changes or disappears.
steps:
1. Select Naturally — Select one naturally occurring thought.
2. Stay Wording — Stay with its exact wording or image as it alters, fragments, loses relevance, or is replaced.
3. Identify Instant — Spot the first instant when no trace can be found.
4. Let It End — Do not resurrect it to verify the ending.
win: The thought reached a point where no trace was findable without being resurrected for checking.
supports:
• Test the assumption; ask what would change your mind.
• Look for one missing fact; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Check the base rate; question absolute words.
• Use a real example; separate possibility from probability.
• Check what you actually know; use current facts.
formula_flow: Select Naturally → Stay Wording → Identify Instant → Let It End
safety:
PAUSE
End observation if tracking becomes obsessive or exhausting.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE RETURN CHAIN
goal: Build attention through a modest daily return instead of heroic sessions.
steps:
1. Choose Attention — Choose one attentional act small enough to repeat daily.
2. Set Cue — Define its cue, duration, and one tiny restart signal.
3. Return Repetition — Each session begins with the final second of yesterday’s intention: ‘return again.’ Protect repetition from heroic increases.
4. Link the Return — A chain is made of modest links.
win: The cue, duration, restart signal, and tomorrow's 'return again' stayed small enough to repeat.
supports:
• Take a short break; close what you do not need.
• Reduce background noise; close extra tabs.
• Park secondary tasks; silence nonessential notifications.
• Put the phone out of reach; mute alerts.
• Keep one task visible; protect one focus block.
formula_flow: Choose Attention → Set Cue → Return Repetition → Link the Return
safety:
PAUSE
Reduce frequency if ongoing sense crowds out sleep, duties, or flexibility.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: NOT FOR, NOT AGAINST
goal: Release the inner pull or push around an experience before deciding what to do.
steps:
1. Check The Pull — Notice whether experience is being pulled closer or pushed away.
2. Relax — Relax the corresponding inner movement without demanding neutrality.
3. Let Content — Let the content remain unowned and unobstructed for a short interval.
4. Act According — Then act according to circumstance, not attraction or aversion.
win: The content remained briefly without being dragged closer or shoved away, then circumstance guided the action.
supports:
• Do one action for your life; limit social media exposure.
• Stop checking their numbers; notice what you cannot see.
• Compare with your past self; return to your own baseline.
• Choose your own measure; track progress by your values.
• Use your own priorities; name one thing already working.
formula_flow: Check The Pull → Relax → Let Content → Act According
safety:
PAUSE
Do not release practical action needed to protect health, rights, or safety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

The content remained briefly without being dragged closer or shoved away, then circumstance guided the action.

• Do one action for your life; limit social media exposure.

title: ERASE THE OBJECT, KEEP THE CONTACT
goal: Let an imagined object lose its labels and shape while attention itself remains.
steps:
1. Stabilise — Stabilise attention on one simple imagined form.
2. Remove Name — Gradually remove its name, meaning, shape, and boundary in that order.
3. Attend Contact — Preserve the sense of attending as the form loses definition.
4. Rest Briefly — Rest with contact that no longer depends on a clear thing.
win: Name, meaning, form, and boundary faded in sequence without the act of attending disappearing.
supports:
• Use one clear sentence; keep the limit simple.
• Do not overexplain the limit; state consequences clearly.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; leave reactions with them.
• Keep consequences realistic; notice resentment as a warning.
• Decide your limit before answering; let guilt pass.
formula_flow: Stabilise → Remove Name → Attend Contact → Rest Briefly
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid object dissolution when prone to derealisation or perceptual instability.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CLOSE THE MICRO-GAPS
goal: Shorten the delay between noticing distraction and returning to the anchor.
steps:
1. Choose Precise — Choose an anchor and notice the precise moment contact breaks.
2. Return Instead — Instead of judging the distraction, shorten the delay before returning.
3. Track Interval — Track the interval between noticing and reconnection.
4. Let Practice — Let practice end after one stretch with visibly fewer or shorter gaps.
win: The gap from 'I wandered' to reconnection became visibly smaller during the practice.
supports:
• Use one screen; return after interruptions.
• Mute alerts; reduce background noise.
• Use a short focus block; clear visual clutter.
• Take a real screen break; reduce nearby noise.
• Keep one task visible; close extra tabs.

1. Identify Part — Spot one part of the present condition that is really adequate: shelter, breath, effort, support, knowledge, or time for the next step.
2. Receive Adequacy — Receive that adequacy without claiming everything is fine.
3. Choose Non — From this base, choose one non-desperate improvement.
win: One present source of adequacy stayed visible while the next change became smaller and less urgent.
supports:
• Do one steadying action; delay the message.
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; lower stimulation for a minute.
• Name the emotion; notice body tension.
• Notice what changed physically; separate feeling from fact.
• Rest before deciding; check the facts separately.
formula_flow: Identify Part → Receive Adequacy → Choose Non
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use contentment to minimise unmet needs or structural harm.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: STUDY THE REACTION, NOT THE CHARACTER
goal: Study a repeated reaction as a pattern, not as proof of your character.
steps:
1. Choose Recurring — Choose a reaction that happens often and remember three times it happened.
2. Read Pattern — For each time, notice the trigger, meaning, body feeling, action, and result.
3. Compare Trusted — Compare the three examples with a trusted idea or guide.
4. Test One Guess — Choose one idea to test. Leave your whole character out of the experiment.
win: Three examples produced triggers, meanings, body cues, actions, and one testable idea without a personality verdict.
supports:
• Do one steadying action; use simple words for the problem.
• Separate feeling from fact; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Check basic needs; rest before deciding.
• Lower nearby noise; name the feeling plainly.
• Wait before sending messages; slow physical pace.
formula_flow: Choose Recurring → Read Pattern → Compare Trusted → Test One Guess
safety:
PAUSE
Stop the study when reflection becomes self-surveillance or shame.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN THE OUTCOME
goal: Do your part fully while releasing the result you cannot command.
steps:
1. Name Action — Name the action within your responsibility.
2. Name Result — Name the result you cannot command.
3. Use Language — Offer the second to God, life, reality, community, or a principle larger than ego—using language authentic to you.
4. Return the Outcome — Then do the first with full care.
win: Responsibility and outcome were separated, so effort could stay wholehearted without pretending control was total.
supports:
• Begin with the easiest part; remove one barrier.
• Choose tiny action; remove one obvious distraction.
• Begin while unsure; restart quickly.
• Touch the first item; lower standards briefly.
• Start with one minute; use one window.
formula_flow: Name Action → Name Result → Use Language → Return the Outcome
safety:
PAUSE
Choose secular release if spiritual framing creates conflict or coercion.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TRACE THE FIRST SPARK
goal: Trace a recurring state back to the earliest condition you can actually notice.
steps:
1. Take Recurring — Take one recurring state and move backward through its chain: current thought, preceding sensation, image, memory, external cue, and hidden tendency.
2. Stop Earliest — Stop at the earliest condition you can really spot.
3. Mark the Spark — Notice the point where future interruption could happen.
win: The chain stopped at one early cue that could become a future interruption point.
supports:
• Give the feeling time to move; rest before deciding.
• Use plain language; delay the message.
• Notice body tension; name the emotion.
• Name the feeling plainly; avoid decisions at peak emotion.
• Separate feeling from fact; notice what changed physically.
formula_flow: Take Recurring → Stop Earliest → Mark the Spark
safety:
PAUSE
Do not force inaccessible memories or invent causes to complete the chain.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: NOT THIS, STILL HERE
goal: Observe body, thought, feeling, and role without calling any one the whole self.
steps:
1. Body — Notice body, sensation, thought, emotion, and role in turn.
2. Keep Perspective — For each say, ‘Observed—therefore not the whole observer.’ Do not claim they are unreal.
3. Rest Unlabelled — After the sequence, rest with what remains unlabelled, then reconnect to name and place.
win: Each layer was noticed, then you reconnected to your current name and place.
supports:
• Notice room temperature; return to one real sound.
• Notice where your body is supported; track one texture.
• Hear one real sound; keep your eyes on something steady.
• Keep eyes open; look around the room.
• Notice three colours; touch a stable surface.
formula_flow: Body → Keep Perspective → Rest Unlabelled
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid negation practices during feeling unreal or disconnected, psychosis, or unstable self-experience.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIND THE FIRST ‘I’
goal: Catch the moment an experience becomes 'mine' or 'about me'.
steps:
1. Experience — Notice an experience before describing it.
2. Wait Moment — Wait for the moment ‘I,’ ‘mine,’ or ‘about me’ attaches.

4. Observe Attachment — Observe the attachment without removing it.
5. Do the Task — The task is detection, not metaphysical victory.
win: The attachment point showed up as a body sensation, image, or location without needing to be removed.

• Use ordinary surroundings; keep movements gentle.
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; wait out the surge.
• Reduce caffeine; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Let breathing stay natural; sip water if it helps.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; give the surge time to pass.

title: CHANGE ONE THING, WATCH ONE FEELING
goal: Change one part of an imagined scene and see which emotion actually moves.
steps:
1. Name Pair — Name two emotions in the mixture and rate each with a simple low, medium, or high—not a number.
2. Hold Scene — Hold the scene steady. Choose only one variable to test: person, time, place, audience, or outcome.
3. Swap Variable — Imagine that one variable changed for ten seconds. Keep every other fact the same.
4. Tag Driver — Notice which emotion moved and which stayed. Tag the changed variable as a likely driver, not a final explanation.
win: Only one variable changed, revealing which feeling shifted and which stayed put.
supports:
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; name the feeling plainly.
• Notice what changed physically; lower nearby noise.
• Check basic needs; slow physical pace.
• Notice body tension; use plain language.
• Give the feeling time to move; let intensity fall.
formula_flow: Name Pair → Hold Scene → Swap Variable → Tag Driver
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use imagined substitutions to rewrite trauma, deny facts, or continue once the scene becomes overwhelming or unreal.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BREAK THE NIGHT'S STORYLINE
goal: Break a night-time storyline into unrelated images that cannot easily continue the plot.
steps:
1. Pick Word — Choose one harmless five-letter word, such as TABLE.
2. Call Image — For the first letter, name a neutral thing beginning with it.
3. Flash Image — Picture it for about two seconds with no action, memory, or story.
4. Jump Letter — Point to the next letter and a completely unrelated image. End after five letters.
win: Five letters produced five separate neutral images without becoming a connected story.
supports:
• Use current facts; ask what would change your mind.
• Check what you actually know; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Ask what would disprove it; check the whole situation.
• Delay the verdict; test the assumption.
• Notice absolute words like always; look for one missing fact.
formula_flow: Pick Word → Call Image → Flash Image → Jump Letter
safety:
PAUSE
Use only while safely resting; never while driving. Stop if images become distressing, compulsive, or disorienting.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE ACTION HAD MANY AUTHORS
goal: Share authorship of an action with the conditions that also helped cause it.
steps:
1. Name Conditions — Review one action and name its conditions: intention, habit, body capacity, other people, resources, timing, culture, and chance.

win: Your contribution remained accountable while habit, capacity, timing, people, culture, and chance re-entered the picture.
supports:

• Lower nearby noise; notice what changed physically.
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; let intensity fall.
• Notice body tension; rest before deciding.
• Give the feeling time to move; wait before sending messages.

PAUSE

title: REMOVE THE NAME BADGES
goal: Set your active roles down briefly, then pick up only the one the next situation needs.
steps:
1. Spot Loudest Role — Notice which role is speaking loudest right now.
2. Set Badges Down — Imagine placing each active badge on a table—parent, worker, partner, achiever, patient, helper, or another role that fits.
3. Pause Without Label — Sit for a short pause without using any badge to answer “Who am I now?”
4. Reclaim One Role — Reclaim only the role the next situation actually needs.
win: Several identity badges became optional for a moment instead of all speaking at once.
supports:
• Change one cue; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; remove easy access.
• Reset without self-criticism; add small friction.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; replace one response.
• Delay the routine; notice the trigger.
formula_flow: Spot Loudest Role → Set Badges Down → Pause Without Label → Reclaim One Role
safety:
PAUSE
Keep grounding and avoid role stripping if identity feels fragile.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CLEAN ACTION, OPEN HANDS
goal: Judge the quality of your action without making the hoped-for result part of the score.
steps:
1. Look Like — Define what right action looks like in process terms: honest words, careful preparation, timely follow-through.
2. Place Outside — Specify the outcome you hope for, then place it outside the scoring system.
3. Judge the Action — Judge today only by whether the action met its standard.
win: Honesty, preparation, and follow-through could be evaluated even while the outcome stayed outside your control.
supports:
• Prepare first; remove one barrier.
• Use one window; choose tiny action.
• Use two minutes; prepare the task in advance.
• Make it visible; restart quickly.
• Start with one minute; reward starting, not finishing.
formula_flow: Look Like → Place Outside → Judge the Action
safety:
PAUSE
Results still matter when they reveal harm, error, or a need to change course.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT REMAINS WHEN REWARD LEAVES?
goal: Find the responsibility that remains even when reward, praise, and punishment disappear.
steps:
1. Name Role — Name your role, the people affected, and the values governing it.
2. Remove Applause — Mentally remove applause, punishment, and personal advantage.
3. Ask Responsibility — Ask which responsibility still stands.
4. Set Role Limit — Convert that answer into a time-bound action and one limit on what the role does not require.
win: One value-based duty survived the removal of personal advantage and became a time-bound action with a clear limit.
supports:
• Keep meaning practical; remove one conflict.
• Use values to choose trade-offs; review what the action costs.
• Remove one conflicting commitment; check whose goal.
• Act before motivation; review the cost.
• Do not wait for motivation; accept the trade-off.
formula_flow: Name Role → Remove Applause → Ask Responsibility → Set Role Limit
safety:
PAUSE
Reject duties that violate safety, ethics, consent, or lawful limits.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SAME VALUE, TWO OUTCOMES
goal: Keep the same value steady across both success and failure.
steps:
1. Imagine Action — Imagine the action succeeding.
2. State Governing — State what that value asks of you next.
3. Imagine Failing — Imagine it failing.
4. State Value — State how the same value responds there.
5. Let Outcome — Let outcome alter strategy, not your ethical centre.
win: The imagined outcome changed strategy, but the value still supplied a next action in either direction.
supports:
• Notice absolute words like always; test the assumption.
• Ask what would change your mind; separate possibility from probability.
• Check the base rate; look for one missing fact.
• Check what you actually know; question absolute words.
• Delay the verdict; ask what else could fit.
formula_flow: Imagine Action → State Governing → Imagine Failing → State Value → Let Outcome
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use equanimity to ignore grief, accountability, or material consequences.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MAKE THE FIRST MOVE DELIBERATELY WRONG
goal: Make an intentionally imperfect start, repair one useful part, and stop polishing.
steps:
1. Throwaway — Open a private mental sandbox and mark it THROWAWAY—NOT FOR SENDING.
2. Make Wrong — Imagine one obviously imperfect start: a clumsy first sentence, rough title, rough mental outline, or unfinished opening.
3. Fix One — Correct exactly one useful part without polishing the rest.
4. Continue Clean — Keep working only if the task now feels editable; otherwise keep the corrected fragment in mind and stop cleanly.
win: The rough beginning became editable after exactly one correction instead of needing to become impressive.
supports:
• Limit checking passes; use actual requirements.
• Define good enough first; stop low-value changes.
• Make rough version; leave minor flaws.
• Separate errors from polish; limit checking.
• Ship useful work; set finish time.
formula_flow: Throwaway → Make Wrong → Fix One → Continue Clean
safety:
PAUSE
Never use deliberate errors in medical, legal, financial, safety-critical, submitted, or live shared work.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ALLY OR SABOTEUR?
goal: Test whether a thought actually clarifies, protects, and leaves you more capable.
steps:
1. Ask Thought — Ask the current thought three questions: Does it clarify the next move.
2. Check Protection — Does it protect something real.
3. Leave Me — Does it leave me more capable afterward.
4. Score Yes — Score each yes or no.
5. Thank Warning — If it fails two, thank the warning and appoint a different inner adviser.
win: A thought that failed most of the test lost its advisory role without needing to be argued out of existence.
supports:
• Shrink the first action; reward starting, not finishing.
• Choose a rough beginning; start before you feel ready.
• Open only what you need; remove one barrier.
• Lower standards briefly; stop planning after one action.
• Prepare first; open the task.

title: THE SIX-LINK FIRE CHAIN
goal: Trace anger backward to the earliest link where fuel can still be removed.
steps:
1. Trace Sequence — Trace the sequence backward: confusion or loss of judgement; anger; frustrated desire; attachment; repeated attention; original cue.
2. Earliest — Find the earliest link still reachable now. Use the simplest true sentence you can.
3. Remove Fuel — Remove fuel there—shift attention, loosen attachment, or revise the demand.
win: The chain led past the heat to one reachable cue, demand, attachment, or attention loop you could change.
supports:
• Clarify the deadline; end with action.
• Ask what they understood; name the desired change.
• Avoid guessing their intent; keep one issue per conversation.
• Separate facts from tone; lead with the point.
• Check the agreed deadline; use one concrete example.

THE SIX-LINK FIRE CHAIN

PLAY TIME
about 1 minute

GOAL
Trace anger backward to the earliest link where fuel can still be removed.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Trace Sequence — Trace the sequence backward: confusion or loss of judgement; anger; frustrated desire; attachment; repeated attention; original cue.
2. Earliest — Find the earliest link still reachable now. Use the simplest true sentence you can.
3. Remove Fuel — Remove fuel there—shift attention, loosen attachment, or revise the demand.

WIN
The chain led past the heat to one reachable cue, demand, attachment, or attention loop you could change.

• Clarify the deadline; end with action.
• Ask what they understood; name the desired change.
• Avoid guessing their intent; keep one issue per conversation.
• Separate facts from tone; lead with the point.
• Check the agreed deadline; use one concrete example.

MIND BEND
Anger may feel like the first event because it is loud. The most changeable link often started several steps earlier.

FORMULA FLOW
Trace Sequence → Earliest → Remove Fuel

SAFETY
PAUSE
Create distance; obtain help whenever aggression or violence risk is present.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE SUSTAINABLE MIDDLE
goal: Move one swinging habit into a middle range you could repeat for two weeks.
steps:
1. Rest Review — Review sleep, food, effort, practice, and rest.
2. Find Area — Find the area swinging between too much and too little.
3. Set Middle — Set a middle range you could repeat for two weeks.
4. Choose Smallest — Use the smallest adjustment that moves into that band today.
win: Sleep, food, effort, practice, or rest shifted toward a sustainable band instead of another extreme.
supports:
• Check what you actually know; ask what would disprove it.
• Separate guess from evidence; delay the verdict.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; check the base rate.
• Check the whole situation; use current facts.
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; check another angle.

safety:
PAUSE

title: DEDICATE THE MOVE
goal: Do one worthwhile action for what it serves beyond immediate reward.
steps:
1. Select Behaviour — Select a behaviour; spot who or what it serves beyond immediate reward: a child, patient, craft, community, future generation, or principle.
2. Act Offering — Do the act as an offering to that recipient.
3. Keep Quality — Keep quality high even if nobody knows.
win: The behaviour kept its quality even though nobody needed to notice or reward it.
supports:
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; wait before sending messages.
• Rest before deciding; slow physical pace.
• Give the feeling time to move; lower nearby noise.
• Delay the message; name the feeling plainly.
• Use plain language; eat, drink, or rest if needed.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not dedicate self-harm, overwork, or boundary violations as virtue.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE WAKING DREAM CHECK
goal: Separate the raw facts of an event from the connections your mind constructed around them.
steps:
1. Take Event — Take one rigid reading of an event.
2. Compare Dream — Compare it with a dream: both organise fragments into a convincing world.
3. Identify Facts — Spot which facts are raw and which connections were constructed.
4. Try Construction — Try one alternate construction and observe how lived experience changes.
win: One alternate interpretation changed lived experience without requiring the original facts to change.
supports:
• Stop checking their numbers; use your own priorities.
• Choose your own measure; do one action for your life.
• Notice what you cannot see; check your own progress.
• Compare with your past self; track progress by your values.
• Keep context visible; limit social media exposure.
formula_flow: Take Event → Compare Dream → Identify Facts → Try Construction
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid dreamlike framing if it increases derealisation or psychotic symptoms.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: STOP RENEWING THE CONSTRUCTION
goal: Stop refreshing one mental construction and let the existing residue fade by itself.
steps:
1. Identify Image — Spot the image, conclusion, or demand being refreshed.
2. Time — For one minute, refuse only the renewal: no new scene, argument, or confirmation.
3. Let Existing — Let existing residue fade at its own rate.
4. Redirect — Redirect the freed attention into a chosen sensory task.
win: No new scene, argument, or confirmation was added while attention moved into a chosen sensory task.
supports:
• Look around the room; reduce sensory input if needed.
• Feel your feet; touch a stable surface.
• Name three visible objects; slow your physical pace.
• Look around slowly; hear one real sound.
• Keep eyes open; name today's date.
formula_flow: Identify Image → Time → Let Existing → Redirect
safety:
PAUSE
Do not withdraw intention from real obligations or safety planning.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN THE PROJECTION TO SENDER
goal: Separate the evidence about someone else from the fear or rule you may be projecting onto it.
steps:
1. Picture Quality — Picture the quality you are assigning outward.
2. Ask Internal — Ask what internal expectation, fear, or rule would make that quality especially visible.
3. Name External — Name the external evidence separately.
4. Keep Facts — Keep what the facts support; return the excess meaning to your own inquiry.
win: External facts kept their weight while unsupported extra meaning returned to your own inquiry.
supports:
• Interrupt the sequence; change the environment.
• Add small friction; reset without self-criticism.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; notice the trigger.
• Replace one response; keep replacement easy.
• Make the new habit easier; interrupt the usual sequence.
formula_flow: Picture Quality → Ask Internal → Name External → Keep Facts
safety:
PAUSE
Projection analysis must not erase another person’s documented behaviour.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DO NOT REPLACE THE LAST THOUGHT
goal: Let one thought end without immediately filling the empty beat with another.
steps:
1. Wait Thought — Wait for a thought to end naturally.
2. Empty — At the first empty beat, resist generating commentary about emptiness.
3. Rest Duration — Rest for the duration available—even a fraction.
4. Let Thought — Let the next thought arise without invitation.
5. Count Gap — Count the gap only after it is over.
win: A real gap appeared before the next thought arrived on its own, even if it lasted only a fraction.
supports:
• Choose tiny action; remove one barrier.
• Make it visible; open only what you need.
• Stop planning after one action; use two minutes.
• Reward starting, not finishing; shrink the first action.
• Skip extra setup; enter through easy work.
formula_flow: Wait Thought → Empty → Rest Duration → Let Thought → Count Gap
safety:
PAUSE
Use external engagement if silence feels frightening or destabilising.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DIFFERENCE INSIDE ONE FIELD
goal: Hold two opposite experiences clearly while noticing the space that contains both.
steps:
1. Contrasting — Notice two contrasting experiences—pleasant and painful, self and other, sound and silence.
2. Hold Distinct — Hold their distinct qualities without merging them.
3. Include Shared — Then include the shared field in which both are present.
4. Let Difference — Let difference remain vivid without translating it into separation.
win: Difference stayed vivid without forcing either side to erase the other or become total separation.
supports:
• Add small friction; notice the trigger.
• Make the new habit easier; reset after slips.
• Keep replacement easy; delay the routine.
• Use the same replacement repeatedly; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Notice the first automatic moment; replace one response.
formula_flow: Contrasting → Hold Distinct → Include Shared → Let Difference
safety:
PAUSE
Use ordinary distinctions when boundaries or safety require clear separation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PRECISE OUTSIDE, QUIET INSIDE
goal: Do the required behaviour precisely while postponing the inner argument about it.
steps:
1. Define — Set the exact external behaviour required.
2. Execute — Execute it with full timing and skill.
3. Imagine Applause — Meanwhile, decline the running argument about authorship, resentment, or imagined applause.
4. Let Body — Allow the body act and the inner courtroom remain closed until the task ends.
win: The external task reached completion before resentment, authorship, or imagined applause got a hearing.
supports:
• Check the facts separately; delay the message.
• Notice what changed physically; lower stimulation for a minute.
• Use plain language; name the emotion.
• Check basic needs; wait before sending messages.
• Use simple words for the problem; lower nearby noise.

safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

steps:
1. Choose Event — Choose a current event and picture the lens being used.
2. Replace Plausible — Replace it with one plausible alternative—not a positive slogan.
3. Act Lens — Spend five minutes acting from the alternate lens and observe changes in body, attention, and available choices.
win: Five minutes under a different interpretation altered at least one body cue, attention pattern, or available choice.
supports:
• Wait before sending messages; check the facts separately.
• Lower nearby noise; notice body tension.
• Do one steadying action; give the feeling time to move.
• Use plain language; notice what changed physically.
• Check basic needs; avoid decisions at peak emotion.

PROOF → Five minutes under a different interpretation altered at least one body cue, attention pattern, or available choice
CHANGE ONE LENS, WATCH THE WORLD
ritual_name: CHANGE ONE LENS, WATCH THE WORLD
ritualText:
CHANGE ONE LENS, WATCH THE WORLD

PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Try one plausible alternative lens and watch what it changes in real behaviour.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Choose Event — Choose a current event and picture the lens being used.
2. Replace Plausible — Replace it with one plausible alternative—not a positive slogan.
3. Act Lens — Spend five minutes acting from the alternate lens and observe changes in body, attention, and available choices.

WIN
Five minutes under a different interpretation altered at least one body cue, attention pattern, or available choice.

• Wait before sending messages; check the facts separately.
• Lower nearby noise; notice body tension.
• Do one steadying action; give the feeling time to move.
• Use plain language; notice what changed physically.
• Check basic needs; avoid decisions at peak emotion.

MIND BEND
A lens feels like reality until another plausible lens changes what becomes visible and doable.

FORMULA FLOW
Choose Event → Replace Plausible → Act Lens

SAFETY
PAUSE
Retain the original lens when evidence confirms danger or wrongdoing.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BOX THE PROBLEM
goal: Shrink a vague problem into its current state, desired state, and measurable gap.
steps:
1. Picture Lines — Picture three lines: CURRENT CONDITION; DESIRED CONDITION; MEASURABLE GAP.
2. Remove History — Remove history unless it changes the gap.
3. Give Problem — Give the problem a time horizon and one owner.
4. Statement — If the statement still contains ‘everything,’ shrink it again.
win: History and 'everything' fell away, leaving a bounded gap with a time horizon and owner.
supports:
• Expect slips and restart quickly; change the environment first.
• Change one cue; reset without self-criticism.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; notice the first automatic moment.
• Change the environment; delay the routine.
• Add small friction; make the new habit easier.
formula_flow: Picture Lines → Remove History → Give Problem → Statement
safety:
PAUSE
Some pain needs witnessing rather than conversion into a problem.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIXED, FLEXIBLE, UNKNOWN, ASSUMED
goal: Sort each barrier by what can be accepted, changed, checked, or tested.
steps:
1. Name — Name every barrier.
2. Mark Category — Mark each barrier as fixed, flexible, unknown, or assumed.
3. Test Assumed — Accept the fixed, negotiate the flexible, investigate the unknown, and test the assumed.
4. Start What Moves — Begin with the highest-impact item whose category permits movement.
win: Every obstacle received a category, and the highest-impact movable one became the starting point.
supports:
• Decide your limit before answering; use a short no.
• Notice resentment as a warning; take time before saying yes.
• Notice resentment early; let guilt pass.
• Delay your answer; leave their reaction with them.
• Repeat without arguing; use one clear sentence.
formula_flow: Name → Mark Category → Test Assumed → Start What Moves
safety:
PAUSE
Reclassify when new evidence changes a limit’s status.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE NO-JUDGEMENT OPTION STORM
goal: Create five genuinely different options before judging whether any of them will work.
steps:
1. Open Possibilities — Generate five options without ranking, explaining, or defending them.
2. Vary Them — Include one conventional, one tiny, one reversible, one collaborative, and one unusual safe option.
3. Delay Judgement — Only after all five exist may feasibility enter the room.
win: Conventional, tiny, reversible, collaborative, and unusual possibilities all existed before feasibility entered.
supports:
• Interrupt the sequence; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Notice the trigger; keep replacement easy.
• Interrupt the usual sequence; add small friction.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; make the new habit easier.
• Reset without self-criticism; notice the first automatic moment.
formula_flow: Open Possibilities → Vary Them → Delay Judgement
safety:
PAUSE
Exclude choices that violate ethics, consent, law, or safety from the start.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DECIDE THE STOPPING LINE FIRST
goal: Decide what evidence is enough before research has a chance to keep moving the line.
steps:
1. State Minimum — Before researching, state the minimum evidence required to choose: number of quotes, critical facts, confidence level, or deadline.
2. Picture Genuinely — Picture what would really reverse the decision.
3. Select Further — When the threshold is met, select; further information needs a new reason for entry.
win: The stopping threshold was defined in advance, reached, and further information needed a new reason to enter.
supports:
• Make the old habit harder; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Notice the trigger; move the cue.
• Keep replacement easy; notice the first automatic moment.
• Change the environment first; add small friction.
• Delay the routine; change the environment.
formula_flow: State Minimum → Picture Genuinely → Select Further
safety:
PAUSE
Raise the threshold for hard to undo or high-stakes decisions.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WORRY HAS OFFICE HOURS
goal: Give worry a later appointment instead of letting it occupy the whole day.
steps:
1. Picture Worry — Picture the worry exactly and schedule a specific review window later today.
2. Add Genuinely — Until then, add only genuinely new facts to the mental note; do not analyse it live.
3. Decide Accept — At the appointment, decide: act, plan, accept, or discard.
4. Close Time — Close on time even if certainty is absent.
win: New facts could be saved, but live analysis waited until the scheduled window and closed on time.
supports:
• Return to current task; set a clear stopping point.
• Name one useful action; limit how long you review it.
• Change rooms; use a short timer.
• End the replay; name one action.
• Leave unsolved questions; ask if any new information exists.

safety:
PAUSE
Use immediate action for urgent safety or time-sensitive problems.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT IS NEW THIS LAP?
goal: Require each new thinking lap to produce something genuinely new.
steps:

2. Name Lap — If nothing specific appears, call the lap REPETITION and keep one short mental summary.

win: When no new fact, distinction, or decision appeared, the loop was named repetition and attention moved elsewhere.
supports:
• Set a stop time; name one useful action.
• Change rooms if possible; use a short timer.
• Set a clear stopping point; return to current task.
• Name one action; change rooms.
• Use your hands; shift attention outward.

title: PAY FOR THE NEXT LAP
goal: Make another thinking lap pay for the time it takes from real life.
steps:
1. Name Lap — Name the exact question you want one more thinking lap to answer. One sentence only.
2. Price Trade — Choose what those three minutes will replace: rest, a message, food, movement, work, or a decision. Say the trade plainly.
3. Buy Three — If the trade is worth it, set three minutes and think only about the named question. If not, close the lap now.
4. Close Toll — When the clock ends, stop without buying another lap. Do the displaced activity or deliberately let it go.
win: The exact question and its trade-off were named before three minutes of thinking were either bought or declined.
supports:
• Return to one physical task; leave unsolved questions.
• End the replay; set a clear stopping point.
• Change rooms if possible; stop solving the unsolvable.
• Name one useful action; ask if any new information exists.
• Stop repeated review; return to current task.
formula_flow: Name Lap → Price Trade → Buy Three → Close Toll
safety:
PAUSE
Never buy another analysis lap with sleep, medication, food, immediate safety, or time-critical responsibilities.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

PLAY TIME
about 90 seconds

GOAL
Make another thinking lap pay for the time it takes from real life.

1. Name Lap — Name the exact question you want one more thinking lap to answer. One sentence only.

title: NEXT PHYSICAL MOVEMENT
goal: Find the first visible body movement that would mean the task has actually begun.
steps:
1. Find First Move — Ask what your body would visibly do first if the task began now.
2. Name It — Name the action and where it would happen in one short phrase.
3. Rehearse — Picture doing only that movement once.
4. Begin — Take that first movement before planning the remainder.
win: The named physical movement happened before the rest of the task was planned.
supports:
• Give the feeling time to move; do one steadying action.
• Wait before sending messages; use plain language.
• Check the facts separately; lower stimulation for a minute.
• Name the emotion; rest before deciding.
• Let intensity fall; delay the message.
formula_flow: Find First Move → Name It → Rehearse → Begin
safety:
PAUSE
Check dependencies first when the movement could create hard to undo consequences.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE REQUEST SPINE
goal: State the situation, its impact, your exact request, and why cooperation helps.
steps:
1. Describe Situation — Say the visible situation.
2. Express Impact — Express its impact.
3. Assert Request — Assert the exact request or no.
4. Reinforce Cooperation — Reinforce why cooperation helps.
5. Picture Sentence — Picture one sentence for each part, then deliver the leanest version.
win: The message reached its request without detouring into accusation, vagueness, or excess explanation.
supports:
• Repeat the same wording calmly; decide your limit before answering.
• Keep consequences realistic; take time before saying yes.
• State consequences clearly; let guilt pass.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; notice resentment as a warning.
• Repeat without arguing; leave their reaction with them.

PAUSE

title: SOFT DELIVERY, SOLID MESSAGE
goal: Keep the message firm while removing unnecessary attack from its delivery.
steps:
1. Remove Attacks — Remove attacks from your wording.
2. Validate Understandable — Show one sign of genuine interest, validate the understandable part of the other experience, and use an easy rather than contemptuous manner.
3. Keep Core — Keep your core message unchanged.
4. Edit Delivery — Gentleness edits delivery, not truth.
win: Interest, validation, and an easier manner changed the tone without changing the core truth.
supports:
• Keep one issue per conversation; separate facts from tone.
• Say the main point first; clarify the deadline.
• Check the agreed deadline; lead with the point.
• Separate tone from facts; use one example.
• Name the desired change; ask for a specific next action.

title: IMPACT IS KNOWN; MOTIVE IS PENDING
goal: Respond to behaviour and impact while leaving the other person's motive undecided.
steps:
1. Separate Unknown — Picture three separate statements: their behaviour; what effect it had; what you do not know about intention.
2. Base — Base your next boundary on behaviour and impact.
3. Leave Motive — Leave motive open until reliable evidence or direct communication updates it.
win: A boundary became possible without needing to prove why the other person did what they did.
supports:
• Notice when checking stops helping; choose a good-enough option.
• Use a decision deadline; ask what is controllable now.
• Set a limit on checking; name what is unknown.
• Accept small risk; act on the safest workable option.
• Delay reassurance seeking; accept a small margin of risk.

PAUSE
Do not use uncertainty about motive to postpone urgent protection.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE FOUR-PART LIMIT
goal: Make a boundary specific enough that your own next action is clear.
steps:
1. State Triggering — State the triggering condition, your limit, the action you will take, and when you will take it.
2. Remove Threats — Remove threats that depend on the other person changing.
3. Practise Line — Practise the line once at speaking volume, then prepare the consequence before delivery.
win: Condition, limit, consequence, and timing were stated without relying on the other person to obey.
supports:
• Protect your capacity; use a short no.
• Notice resentment as a warning; keep consequences realistic.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; let guilt pass.
• Use one clear sentence; do not debate your limit.
• Notice resentment early; keep the limit simple.
formula_flow: State Triggering → Remove Threats → Practise Line
safety:
PAUSE
Seek safety planning before setting boundaries with a violent or controlling person.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ROTATE THE CHAIR
goal: View the same event from your seat, their possible seat, a neutral seat, and future-you.
steps:
1. Describe Event — Describe the event from your position.
2. Move Seats — Move seats and say what the other person might perceive, labelling guesses.
3. Watch Behaviour — Stand as a neutral observer and keep only observable behaviour.
4. Ask Future — Finally, ask what future-you would wish had happened next.
win: Facts and guesses became easier to separate after the event was seen from four different positions.
supports:
• Keep one issue per conversation; confirm who will do what.
• Say the main point first; end with action.
• Check the request; ask for a specific next action.
• Check the agreed deadline; name the desired change.
• Avoid guessing their intent; use shorter sentences when tense.
formula_flow: Describe Event → Move Seats → Watch Behaviour → Ask Future
safety:
PAUSE
Skip the other-person chair if it invites self-blame after abuse.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CARE WITHOUT CARRYING
goal: Offer the compassionate action that is yours without taking over someone else's emotional work.
steps:
1. Separate Feelings — Name the other person’s feeling and your own current feeling separately.
2. Locate Relative — Locate each relative to your body.
3. Ask Compassionate — Ask what compassionate action is actually yours and what emotional work remains theirs.
4. Care Without Carrying — Offer the first without absorbing the second.
win: Their feeling and yours stayed separate, and support stopped at the edge of your real responsibility.
supports:
• Let guilt pass; offer only genuine options.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; do not overexplain the limit.
• Protect your capacity; keep consequences realistic.
• Delay your answer; notice resentment as a warning.
• Do not debate your limit; take time before saying yes.

title: THE FIVE-BRICK REPAIR
goal: Turn an apology into a specific repair that can be seen over time.
steps:
1. Build Repair — Build five bricks in order: the event without spin; the impact without defence; your responsibility without dilution; the unmet need; one concrete repair action.
2. Ask Evidence — Decide what changed behaviour would look like over time.
3. Make It Real — Treat the apology as the doorway and the changed behaviour as the proof.
win: Event, impact, responsibility, unmet need, and one repair action formed a path beyond the words 'I'm sorry'.
supports:
• Name the exact mistake; notice evidence of capability.
• Prefer repair; drop self-punishment.
• Keep guilt precise; choose one repair.
• Do not punish yourself for learning; separate guilt from responsibility.
• Use equal standards; name what was outside your control.

title: SAY IT IN YOUR MIND. DO NOT SEND IT.
goal: Say the unsent truth in your mind, then leave contact alone for a full day.
steps:
1. See The Person — Imagine the person in front of you.
2. Say What Happened — In your mind, say what happened, what you felt, what you needed, and what you now choose to release.
3. Do Not Edit — Let the message be honest, but do not plan harm.
4. Wait — Do not contact the person for twenty-four hours. Let the message stay only in your mind.
win: The message expressed what happened, felt, mattered, and could be released without becoming an immediate send.
supports:
• Notice the first automatic moment; move the cue.
• Interrupt the sequence; notice the trigger.
• Interrupt the usual sequence; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Reduce easy access to triggers; reset after slips.
• Keep replacement easy; change the environment first.

safety:
PAUSE
Stop and seek support if the exercise increases revenge thoughts, fear, or trauma.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TWO CHAIRS, NO TELEPATHY
goal: Imagine both sides of a conversation without pretending you can know the other mind.
steps:
1. Picture Positions — Imagine two positions facing each other in your mind.
2. Speak Position — State your own position in first person.
3. Shift View — Imagine the other position and answer without pretending you know their mind.
4. Return To Facts — Come back to your view and separate facts from guesses.
win: Your position, their possible position, and the observable facts ended in separate places.
supports:
• Reset after slips; change the environment.
• Replace one response; notice the trigger.
• Change one cue; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Add small friction; keep replacement easy.
• Change the environment first; move the cue.

title: MOVE THE CHARGE INTO A CONTAINER
goal: Move anger or alarm through controlled physical effort without rehearsing harm.
steps:
1. Choose Release — Choose shaking, wall-free pushing motions, stamping, stretching, or strong walking.
2. Set Limit — Decide a safe maximum intensity and ten controlled repetitions.
3. Move — Complete the repetitions without rehearsing violence.
4. Find Settling — Stand still afterward until you notice the earliest easing signal.
win: The chosen repetitions stayed within a safe limit and ended at the first detectable easing signal.
supports:
• Reduce caffeine; stay somewhere physically safe.
• Wait out the surge; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Sip water if it helps; loosen your shoulders.
• Let breathing stay natural; stop body scanning.
• Keep movements gentle; use ordinary surroundings.

safety:
PAUSE
Stop for pain, dizziness, aggression, or loss of action control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MOVE THE HEAVIEST WORD
goal: Change which word carries the weight and notice how the sentence's meaning shifts.
steps:
1. Say Alarm — Choose one short alarm sentence.
2. Shift Stress — Say it quietly several times, moving emphasis to one different word per round. Keep pitch and speed comfortable.
3. Find Weight — Notice which emphasis changes the meaning or body response most. Focus only on that word.
4. Keep Signal — Keep the weighted word as information; stop the repetitions without debating the whole sentence.
win: One emphasized word changed the body response enough to reveal where the alarm sentence was really loaded.
supports:
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; lower nearby noise.
• Name the emotion; check basic needs.
• Wait before sending messages; rest before deciding.
• Delay the message; give the feeling time to move.
• Name the feeling plainly; use simple words for the problem.
formula_flow: Say Alarm → Shift Stress → Find Weight → Keep Signal
safety:
PAUSE
Use silent emphasis if speaking is unsafe; stop for voice strain, breathing difficulty, or rising panic.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

Change which word carries the weight and notice how the sentence's meaning shifts.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Say Alarm — Choose one short alarm sentence.
2. Shift Stress — Say it quietly several times, moving emphasis to one different word per round. Keep pitch and speed comfortable.
3. Find Weight — Notice which emphasis changes the meaning or body response most. Focus only on that word.
4. Keep Signal — Keep the weighted word as information; stop the repetitions without debating the whole sentence.

WIN
One emphasized word changed the body response enough to reveal where the alarm sentence was really loaded.

• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; lower nearby noise.
• Name the emotion; check basic needs.
• Wait before sending messages; rest before deciding.
• Delay the message; give the feeling time to move.
• Name the feeling plainly; use simple words for the problem.

MIND BEND
A sentence can feel globally threatening when one word is doing most of the emotional work.

Say Alarm → Shift Stress → Find Weight → Keep Signal

SAFETY
PAUSE
Use silent emphasis if speaking is unsafe; stop for voice strain, breathing difficulty, or rising panic.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CHANGE THE OBJECT, MARK THE RELEASE
goal: Mark a release with one safe physical transformation and keep the responsibility that remains.
steps:
1. Picture Safe — Picture or select a safe symbol for what you are relinquishing.
2. Choose Transformation — Choose a transformation that fits: fold, seal, store, shred, bury where lawful, or dissolve safely.
3. Name Responsibility — Name what is ending and what responsibility remains.
4. Mark the Release — Complete the physical change once.
win: The symbol changed once, making the ending visible without pretending every consequence disappeared.
supports:
• Move the cue; make the new habit easier.
• Change the environment; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Add small friction; reduce easy access to triggers.
• Make the old habit harder; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Replace one response; reset without self-criticism.

safety:
PAUSE
Never burn, bury, ingest, or destroy items unsafely or illegally.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: IMAGINE THE FEELING’S SHAPE
goal: Give the feeling a shape, then change one visual feature and notice the effect.
steps:
1. Assign Colour — Without aiming for beauty, assign the state a colour, texture, shape, size, and position in your mind.
2. Add Boundary — Add a boundary, pressure source, and possible exit route.
3. Change One Feature — Change one visual property and notice whether the inner state shifts.
win: Colour, texture, size, boundary, pressure, or exit changed and the inner state either moved or stayed put.
supports:
• Do not debate your limit; use a short no.
• Delay your answer; leave reactions with them.
• Protect your capacity; keep the limit simple.
• Offer alternatives only if genuine; repeat the same wording calmly.
• Let guilt pass; notice resentment early.

2. State Anger — State the anger plainly without rehearsing violence or revenge.
3. Find Boundary — Name the boundary, need, or value underneath the heat.
4. Choose Safe Action — Select one action that protects the boundary without causing damage.

WIN
The heat was named without revenge, and one non-damaging action protected the need or value beneath it.

• Repeat the same wording calmly; use a short no.
• Do not overexplain the limit; offer alternatives only if genuine.
• Use one clear sentence; leave their reaction with them.
• Notice resentment as a warning; keep the limit simple.
• Let guilt pass; do not debate your limit.

MIND BEND
Anger often points to a crossed line. The useful information survives even when the urge to punish is removed.

FORMULA FLOW
Create Space → State Anger → Find Boundary → Choose Safe Action

SAFETY
PAUSE
Leave immediately and get help if there is risk of harming anyone or damaging property.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CROSS OUT THE EXPIRED FUTURE
goal: Retire a prediction the moment the condition that made it relevant has ended.
steps:
1. Picture Prediction — Picture the prediction and the exact condition that makes it obsolete: date passed, result known, action completed, evidence changed.
2. Imagine Line — When that condition arrives, imagine a line through the prediction and picture the word EXPIRED.
3. Remove Vote — It may remain historically visible, but it receives no further vote.
win: The forecast was mentally stamped expired and stopped influencing present choices once its deadline or evidence changed.
supports:
• Check the base rate; use a real example.
• Notice absolute words like always; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Check the whole situation; look for one missing fact.
• Delay the verdict; check what you actually know.
• Use current facts; question absolute words.
formula_flow: Picture Prediction → Imagine Line → Remove Vote
safety:
PAUSE
Reopen only when genuinely new evidence creates a new forecast.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PUT THE MEMORY BACK IN PAST TENSE
goal: Put one memory segment into past tense while inserting present facts between loaded lines.
steps:
1. Use Happened — Retell one short segment using was, happened, had, and then.
2. Ground Between — After every emotionally loaded sentence, insert three present facts: your present location, the current year, and what choice exists now.
3. Finish Moment — Finish with: ‘That ended; this moment is different.’
win: The retelling repeatedly returned to current place, year, and available choice before ending in today's reality.
supports:
• Slow physical pace; do one steadying action.
• Lower stimulation for a minute; name the feeling plainly.
• Eat, drink, or rest if needed; separate feeling from fact.
• Rest before deciding; lower nearby noise.
• Name the emotion; check the facts separately.
formula_flow: Use Happened → Ground Between → Finish Moment
safety:
PAUSE
Do not retell alone if the memory overwhelms sense of where you are.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: BREAK THE DEADLINE MONOLITH
goal: Turn one looming deadline into separate usable work blocks with visible finishes.
steps:
1. Count Usable — Count the usable work blocks remaining, subtracting sleep and fixed duties.
2. Give Block — Give each block one deliverable with a visible finish.
3. Place Buffers — Place buffers before the final deadline.
4. Start Earliest — Start the earliest window; refuse to mentally carry later windows inside it.
win: Sleep and fixed duties were respected, buffers existed, and only the earliest work window was mentally active.
supports:
• Pick the reversible option first; set a decision deadline.
• Keep new facts separate; set a deadline.
• Choose the option you can support; stop extra research.
• Choose by the strongest evidence; avoid reopening without new facts.
• Name must-haves; limit the options.

title: TURN ANTICIPATION INTO INVENTORY
goal: Convert repeated future scenes into preparation until they stop producing anything new.
steps:
1. Repeat Extract — Each time the same future scene repeats, extract one actionable item: question, document, rehearsal, route, support, or if-then link.
2. Add Checklist — Add it to a checklist.

win: Each useful replay became a checklist item, and repetition was closed once no new preparation emerged.
supports:
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; loosen your shoulders.
• Use ordinary surroundings; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Keep your body supported; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; wait out the surge.
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; keep movements gentle.

title: THE AFTERSHOCK CLOCK
goal: Give post-event activation a recovery window before letting it rewrite what the event meant.
steps:
1. Set Reasonable — Set a reasonable after-event window during which shakiness, mental loops, fatigue, or emotion are expected echoes.
2. Picture Time — Picture its end time.
3. Notice Sensations — Until then, keep sensations but forbid them from changing your meaning of what happened.
4. Reassess — Reassess after recovery and sleep where possible.
win: Shakiness, fatigue, or looping were treated as echoes until the chosen reassessment point rather than fresh evidence.
supports:
• Keep movements gentle; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Unclench your jaw; let breathing stay natural.
• Keep your body supported; wait out the surge.
• Reduce caffeine; sip water if it helps.
• Stop body scanning; unclench your jaw and shoulders.

3. Notice Sensations — Until then, keep sensations but forbid them from changing your meaning of what happened.
4. Reassess — Reassess after recovery and sleep where possible.

Shakiness, fatigue, or looping were treated as echoes until the chosen reassessment point rather than fresh evidence.

• Keep movements gentle; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Unclench your jaw; let breathing stay natural.
• Keep your body supported; wait out the surge.
• Reduce caffeine; sip water if it helps.
• Stop body scanning; unclench your jaw and shoulders.

PAUSE

title: PUT THE YEARS BACK BETWEEN THEM
goal: Restore the real time distance between events that currently feel piled together.
steps:
1. Date Events — Picture the dates of the events that currently feel piled together.
2. Scale Distance — Give equal physical space to equal spans of time; do not place every event in one crowded cluster.
3. Present — Notice TODAY at the correct distance and name one fact that belongs only to now.
4. Recheck Urgency — Look again at the oldest event and rate how immediate it feels after the spacing is restored.
win: Older events moved back along the timeline, and one fact belonging only to today regained its proper place.
supports:
• Ignore imagined regret; reduce the options.
• Keep new facts separate; limit the options.
• Choose the option you can support; commit once chosen.
• Choose reversible first; set a deadline.
• Ask what failure would cost; stop extra research.
formula_flow: Date Events → Scale Distance → Present → Recheck Urgency
safety:
PAUSE
Stop and reorient to the room if the timeline makes the past feel more present.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: A NOTE FROM TOMORROW MORNING
goal: Let tomorrow-you protect one thing that tonight's urge may forget.
steps:
1. Picture Tomorrow — Picture tomorrow-you after tonight’s urge has passed. Ask what one thing they want protected: sleep, money, sobriety, dignity, preparation, or safety.
2. Date It — Mentally sign the request with tomorrow’s date.
3. Place the Contract — Bring that promise to mind exactly where the immediate choice happens.
win: A dated promise about sleep, money, sobriety, dignity, preparation, or safety reached the exact choice point.
supports:
• Drink some water; change rooms if possible.
• Eat if hungry; change locations.
• Leave the trigger; make access less convenient.
• Tell someone if the urge spikes; ride the peak.
• Delay ten minutes; avoid bargaining.

safety:
PAUSE
Use live support when an urge threatens serious harm or relapse.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TWENTY SECONDS BEFORE THE STORY
goal: Describe the body's physics before choosing an emotion label or story.
steps:
1. Name Causes — For twenty seconds, ban emotion names and causes.
2. Describe Geometry — Say only geometry and physics: shape, temperature, pressure, texture, direction, pulse.
3. Choose Smallest — At the bell, choose the smallest plain word that fits, or keep it unnamed if none does.
win: Shape, temperature, pressure, texture, direction, and pulse were noticed before a simple feeling word was allowed in.
supports:
• Notice what changed physically; use plain language.
• Let intensity fall; slow physical pace.
• Name the emotion; separate feeling from fact.
• Lower nearby noise; wait before sending messages.
• Rest before deciding; lower stimulation for a minute.

safety:
PAUSE
Stop internal focus if it triggers panic, feeling unreal or disconnected, or pain concern.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THIRD-PERSON OWNERSHIP TEST
goal: Step back from the mind's content without stepping away from the action you own.
steps:
1. Describe Event — Frame the moment once as ‘this mind is predicting…’ or ‘the system is producing…’.
2. Change — Notice what changes in intensity, responsibility, and choice.
3. Return Person — Then return to first person for the action you really own: ‘I will…’.
4. Loosen the Grammar — Distance the content, not agency.
win: The prediction was described at a distance, then first-person agency returned exactly where behaviour began.
supports:
• Lower standards briefly; shrink the first action.
• Reward starting, not finishing; use one window.
• Remove one obvious distraction; prepare first.
• Cut the task; enter through easy work.
• Restart quickly; make it visible.
formula_flow: Describe Event → Change → Return Person → Loosen the Grammar
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if altered pronouns increase estrangement from self.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: LET THE IMAGE FIND ITS LAST FRAME
goal: Let a troubling image reach its own final frame without adding verbal commentary.
steps:
1. Bring Image — Bring up the image gently and prohibit verbal commentary.
2. Allow Move — Allow it to move at its own speed until it reaches a stable frame or natural ending.
3. Check Your Position — Notice whether your position, distance, or available action changes.
4. Use Sensory — Reorient afterward using present sensory facts.
win: The image moved to a stable ending and your present sensory surroundings were restored afterward.
supports:
• Keep eyes open; touch a stable surface.
• Feel your feet; look around the room.
• Notice temperature and texture; feel both feet.
• Feel the chair; notice room temperature.
• Name three visible objects; keep your eyes on something steady.
formula_flow: Bring Image → Allow Move → Check Your Position → Use Sensory
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use alone with traumatic imagery, hallucinations, or destabilisation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: NO-CONCEPT MINUTE
goal: Spend one minute with direct sensation before concepts are allowed to explain it.
steps:
1. Set Brief — Set a brief interval.
2. Name Comparisons — During it, do not create causes, labels, comparisons, or solutions.
3. Attend Direct — Attend to direct colour, sound, contact, and movement.
4. Let Sensory — If a concept appears, acknowledge ‘explanation’ and let the sensory world continue.
win: Colour, sound, contact, and movement continued while labels, comparisons, and solutions were treated as later additions.
supports:
• Notice temperature and texture; feel the chair.
• Slow your physical pace; track one texture.
• Return to one real sound; notice three colours.
• Notice room temperature; keep your eyes on something steady.
• Name three visible objects; feel your feet.
formula_flow: Set Brief → Name Comparisons → Attend Direct → Let Sensory
safety:
PAUSE
Concept fasting must not delay necessary decisions or medical care.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TURN THE LABEL INTO MOTION
goal: Translate a fixed label into the moving behaviours and conditions underneath it.
steps:
1. Take Identity — Take the identity or label word dominating the moment.
2. Translate Active — Translate it into active, time-specific verbs ending in -ing: withdrawing, scanning, grieving, protecting, predicting.
3. Ask Strengthens — Ask what starts, strengthens, interrupts, and ends that process.
win: The identity word became active verbs with clear triggers, intensifiers, interruptions, and endings.
supports:
• Delay the routine; keep replacement easy.
• Add small friction; reset after slips.
• Change the environment first; interrupt the sequence.
• Make the old habit harder; change one cue.
• Move the cue; replace one response.
formula_flow: Take Identity → Translate Active → Ask Strengthens
safety:
PAUSE
Do not discard formal diagnoses needed for treatment or access to support.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

• Add small friction; reset after slips.
• Change the environment first; interrupt the sequence.
• Make the old habit harder; change one cue.
• Move the cue; replace one response.

title: MUTE THE INNER SUBTITLES
goal: Do one ordinary activity without narrating it from inside your head.
steps:
1. Choose Washing — Choose washing, walking, eating, or dressing.
2. Duration — For the duration, omit internal narration and meet only sensation and movement.
3. Rejoin Activity — When commentary resumes, do not answer it; rejoin the activity at the next contact point.
win: Commentary returned, went unanswered, and attention rejoined the next real contact point of the activity.
supports:
• Name today's date; look around the room.
• Keep your eyes on something steady; notice temperature and texture.
• Return to one real sound; slow your physical pace.
• Hear one real sound; keep eyes open.
• Feel both feet; notice room temperature.
formula_flow: Choose Washing → Duration → Rejoin Activity
safety:
PAUSE
Keep internal language available for safety-critical tasks.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MEANING ON HOLD
goal: Delay meaning until facts from several channels are actually present.
steps:
1. Hold Event — Notice the event without explaining it.
2. Find Facts — Find three facts from different channels—what was said, what was observed, what occurred over time.
3. Name Meaning — Until all three exist, name every meaning temporary.
4. Assign Narrowest — Then assign the narrowest meaning supported.
win: Observed facts and timing came first; the final meaning stayed no broader than the evidence.
supports:
• Interrupt the usual sequence; change the environment.
• Interrupt the sequence; move the cue.
• Remove easy access; reset without self-criticism.
• Delay the routine; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Notice the trigger; reduce easy access to triggers.
formula_flow: Hold Event → Find Facts → Name Meaning → Assign Narrowest
safety:
PAUSE
Do not postpone action when even one fact confirms urgent danger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: COOL THE WORDS, KEEP THE FACTS
goal: Replace inflammatory language with the exact frequency, loss, or behaviour it refers to.
steps:
1. Spot Absolutes — Catch any absolute or inflammatory word in your account.
2. Cool The Words — Replace each one with a precise fact: ‘always’ becomes the actual frequency; ‘destroyed’ becomes the specific loss; ‘evil’ becomes the observed behaviour.
3. Read Action — Say the cooler version once and notice what action it supports.
win: The cooler account kept the facts and produced a more specific next action.
supports:
• Stay somewhere physically safe; unclench your jaw.
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; sit somewhere safe.
• Loosen your shoulders; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Reduce caffeine; use ordinary surroundings.
• Give the surge time to pass; stop body scanning.
formula_flow: Spot Absolutes → Cool The Words → Read Action
safety:
PAUSE
Retain strong moral language when accurate naming is necessary.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ONE WORD, ONE BREATH, RELEASE
goal: Let one temporary word carry the issue for a breath, then leave the label empty.
steps:
1. Choose Temporary — Choose a temporary word that holds the issue: betrayal, pressure, uncertainty, loss.
2. Say During — Say it once during a natural breath, feel its weight, and let the word leave with the breath’s end.
3. Keep One Name — Do not replace it with another label for thirty seconds.
win: The word ended with the breath and no replacement label was supplied for the next thirty seconds.
supports:
• Delay reassurance; ask what is controllable now.
• Accept small risk; leave one question unanswered.
• Avoid reopening settled choices; name what is unknown.
• Act with uncertainty; use a decision deadline.
• Choose a good-enough option; use a deadline.
formula_flow: Choose Temporary → Say During → Keep One Name
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid compression when important complexity must be communicated.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CAPTURE THE MODEL’S MISS
goal: Preserve the original prediction when reality surprises it.
steps:

• Question absolute words; use current facts.
• Add the missing context; separate guess from evidence.
• Notice absolute words like always; delay major conclusions when upset.

title: MAKE FEAR NAME A DEADLINE
goal: Make fear state exactly what should happen, by when, and how confident it is.
steps:
1. Pin Forecast — Restate the fear as one visible or audible prediction—not a vague catastrophe.
2. Set Clock — Give the prediction a real time window.
3. Score Odds — Set confidence on a 0–100 scale before checking anything.
4. Observe Safely — Use only a naturally occurring safe observation; never manufacture a test.
5. Update Odds — Use the result to update confidence in either direction.
win: The prediction gained a visible outcome, deadline, and pre-check confidence that could later move with naturally occurring evidence.
supports:
• Separate guess from evidence; look for one missing fact.
• Check the whole situation; question absolute words.
• Test the assumption; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Ask what else could fit; check what you actually know.
• Use a real example; ask what would disprove it.
formula_flow: Pin Forecast → Set Clock → Score Odds → Observe Safely → Update Odds
safety:
PAUSE
Do not test danger, invade privacy, or repeat the observation to chase certainty.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CONFIDENCE IS NOT EVIDENCE
goal: Keep felt certainty on a different meter from the quality of the evidence.
steps:
1. Rate Sure — Rate how sure you feel from 0–100.
2. Rate Evidence — Independently rate evidence quality using source reliability, directness, and recency.
3. Separate Meters — Picture the two scores on separate meters so certainty cannot masquerade as evidence.
4. Follow Evidence — Let the evidence meter choose the action; treat the confidence meter as a feeling to notice, not a vote.
win: The action followed source reliability, directness, and recency rather than the number measuring how sure you felt.
supports:
• Start smaller; do the easiest useful part.
• Choose tiny action; skip extra setup.
• Cut the task; open only what you need.
• Open the task; begin while unsure.
• Use a visible cue; start physically.
formula_flow: Rate Sure → Rate Evidence → Separate Meters → Follow Evidence
safety:
PAUSE
Urgent protective instincts may require action while evidence is gathered.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: GIVE THE FORECAST EDGES
goal: Give a forecast enough detail that both success and failure can be recognised later.
steps:
1. Sharpen Forecast — Sharpen the prediction with who, what visible event, exact time window, location, and clear threshold.
2. Define — Define the sign of the event not happening.
3. Set Review — Set a review date and refuse to score the prediction before then.
win: Who, what, when, where, threshold, non-event sign, and review date made the prediction scoreable.
supports:
• Delay the routine; interrupt the sequence.
• Remove easy access; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Move the cue; keep replacement easy.
• Replace one response; change the environment first.
• Add small friction; expect slips and restart quickly.

safety:

title: THREE ACTIVE FUTURES ONLY
goal: Keep only three future predictions active enough to influence the decision.
steps:
1. Picture Predictions — Picture the three predictions currently most relevant.
2. Enter Retiring — Any new prediction may enter only by retiring one, merging with one, or proving more useful for the decision.
3. Retire One — Mentally remove any retired prediction from view.
4. Act Portfolio — Act from the remaining three rather than unlimited mental possibilities.
win: Every extra forecast had to replace, merge with, or outperform one already on the mental board.
supports:
• Make the old habit harder; add small friction.
• Keep replacement easy; replace one response.
• Change the environment first; make the new habit easier.
• Change the environment; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Reset without self-criticism; interrupt the sequence.

title: PUT AN EXPIRY DATE ON THE CONCLUSION
goal: Give a conclusion a review date so stale evidence cannot keep directing behaviour.
steps:
1. Estimate Quickly — Estimate how quickly the conclusion’s evidence can become stale.
2. Give Renewal — Give it a renewal date plus the data required then.
3. Use Temporaryly — Until review, use it temporaryly; after expiry, it must be renewed by current evidence before influencing behaviour.
win: The belief received an expiry point, renewal data, and temporary status until current evidence earns another term.
supports:
• Open the task; restart quickly.
• Begin while unsure; choose tiny action.
• Skip extra setup; remove one obvious distraction.
• Prepare the task in advance; open only what you need.
• Reward starting, not finishing; start before you feel ready.

safety:
PAUSE
Stable facts do not need artificial expiry simply to reduce discomfort.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SAME FACTS, THREE ASSUMPTIONS
goal: Run the same facts through different assumptions and look for the action that survives them.
steps:
1. Keep Observations — Keep all observations fixed.
2. Reframe Three Ways — Run the same facts through three different assumptions about motive, capability, or context.
3. Identify Action — For each, spot the one simple action it recommends.
4. Compare Action — Compare which action remains robust across versions.
win: Three interpretations produced three recommendations, making the robust action easier to see without settling motive first.
supports:
• Ask what would disprove it; separate guess from evidence.
• Check the whole situation; separate possibility from probability.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; use a real example.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; question absolute words.
• Test the assumption; notice absolute words like always.
formula_flow: Keep Observations → Reframe Three Ways → Identify Action → Compare Action
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid invented alternatives that contradict established evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

goal: Wait only for future information that can genuinely change the choice.
steps:

win: The needed evidence, arrival time, and action consequence were defined, leaving unrelated research without a reason to continue.

title: KEEP THE THREAT, ADD THE PERIPHERY
goal: Keep the threat in view while widening attention to what is happening around it.
steps:
1. Hold Trigger — Hold the trigger at a manageable centre.
2. Look Away — Without looking away, name five simultaneous peripheral details—colour, distance, movement, light, geometry.
3. Let Central — Let central and surrounding information coexist until the scene feels larger than the alarm.
win: Five peripheral details joined the central trigger until the scene contained more information than alarm alone.
supports:
• Choose one target; finish or park one open loop.
• Use one screen; reduce background noise.
• Silence nonessential notifications; close extra tabs.
• Close what you do not need; mute alerts.
• Park secondary tasks; take a short break.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not keep a dangerous cue in view when withdrawal is the safer action.
