title: ZOOM LENS TRAINING
goal: Practise moving attention between tiny detail and the whole scene.
steps:
1. Imagine Shape — Picture one simple shape.
2. Zoom Detail — Spend ten slow counts on one tiny feature.
3. Widen View — Spend ten counts on the whole shape and the space around it.
4. Reverse — Move back to detail, then choose the view that best fits your task.
win: You could zoom in, zoom out, and deliberately choose the view that fit the task.
supports:
• Delay the verdict; question absolute words.
• Check what you actually know; use a real example.
• Check the base rate; test the assumption.
• Notice absolute words like always; ask what else could fit.
• Check the whole situation; ask what would change your mind.

title: VIVID IS NOT IMPORTANT
goal: Separate how noticeable information feels from how much it actually changes the decision.
steps:
1. Score Information — Score the information on two separate axes: how noticeable it feels and how much it changes the choice.

title: GROUNDING ANCHOR RELAY
goal: Rotate through several grounding channels and keep the one that restores the clearest present contact.
steps:
1. Select Different — Select four anchors from different systems: visual line, distant sound, contact pressure, joint position.
2. Switch Getting — Spend a short interval with each and switch before getting used to it empties it.

win: Visual, auditory, pressure, and joint cues were tested before one channel became the final anchor.
supports:
• Notice temperature and texture; slow your physical pace.
• Track one texture; feel the chair.
• Return to one real sound; touch a stable surface.
• Feel your feet; keep eyes open.
• Hear one real sound; name three visible objects.

safety:
PAUSE
Use fewer anchors if switching itself increases overload.

title: BRAID THE SIGNALS
goal: Let two competing signals share attention before deciding which one matters.
steps:
1. Choose Signals — Choose the two signals fighting for attention.
2. Alternate B — Alternate A–B–A–B at a slow fixed rhythm.
3. Hold Time — Then hold both at the same time for one interval, noticing difference without choosing.
4. Decide After — Decide only after the braid is complete.
win: A–B alternation became simultaneous awareness, and the decision waited until both signals had been fully represented.
supports:
• Use one screen; keep one task visible.
• Reduce nearby noise; finish or park one open loop.
• Use one window at a time; mute alerts.
• Clear visual clutter; silence nonessential notifications.
• Choose one target; take a real screen break.
formula_flow: Choose Signals → Alternate B → Hold Time → Decide After
safety:
PAUSE
Do not braid a safety alarm with pressure to ignore it.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: STAMP THE ENDING INTO THE SENSES
goal: Give a truly finished topic one repeatable sensory ending and a clear return time.
steps:
1. Choose A Finish — Choose one finish you can repeat: wash your hands, hear a soft sound, touch a doorframe, or change the light.
2. Pair It — Pair it with one short answer in your mind and a time to think about it again.
3. Close It — Use the sensory finish only when the topic is truly closed.
win: The subject closed with a physical cue, one short mental answer, and a defined point for any future review.
supports:
• Name three visible objects; track one texture.
• Name today's date; notice temperature and texture.
• Keep eyes open; slow your physical pace.
• Feel both feet; touch a stable surface.
• Reduce sensory input if needed; notice three colours.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not close matters that still require urgent action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MOVE NOVELTY TO THE RIGHT TEAM
goal: Move novelty into the useful task instead of letting novelty pull you away from it.
steps:
1. Identify Novelty — Notice what kind of novelty is stealing attention.
2. Reassign Novelty — Mentally add variety to the desired task by changing order, challenge, or approach.
3. Keep Goal — Keep the goal constant while refreshing the route.
4. Re-enter — Picture the first refreshed move and begin there.
win: The goal stayed fixed while order, challenge, or approach changed enough to refresh the first move.
supports:
• Clear visual clutter; take a real screen break.
• Mute alerts; use a short focus block.
• Choose one target; reduce nearby noise.
• Return to one target; take a short break.
• Use one screen; put the phone out of reach.

safety:
PAUSE
Avoid novelty additions that reduce accuracy or safety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

ritualText:
MOVE NOVELTY TO THE RIGHT TEAM

PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Move novelty into the useful task instead of letting novelty pull you away from it.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Identify Novelty — Notice what kind of novelty is stealing attention.
2. Reassign Novelty — Mentally add variety to the desired task by changing order, challenge, or approach.
3. Keep Goal — Keep the goal constant while refreshing the route.
4. Re-enter — Picture the first refreshed move and begin there.

WIN
The goal stayed fixed while order, challenge, or approach changed enough to refresh the first move.

• Clear visual clutter; take a real screen break.
• Mute alerts; use a short focus block.
• Choose one target; reduce nearby noise.
• Return to one target; take a short break.
• Use one screen; put the phone out of reach.

MIND BEND
Novelty-seeking is not always opposition to the task. Sometimes the brain is asking the route to change while the destination can stay.

FORMULA FLOW
Identify Novelty → Reassign Novelty → Keep Goal → Re-enter

SAFETY
PAUSE
Avoid novelty additions that reduce accuracy or safety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CLOSE THE ATTENTION TABS
goal: Close, schedule, delegate, or resume abandoned items until only one stays active.
steps:
1. Visit — Briefly bring each abandoned item to mind.
2. Name Next Move — For each, choose close, schedule, delegate, or resume.
3. Do Not Perform — Do not work on the items during the sweep.
4. End Active — Keep one active item and one short mental return phrase for the rest.
win: The sweep ended with one current item and a short return phrase for everything else.
supports:
• Close what you do not need; return to one target.
• Choose one target; keep one task visible.
• Use one screen; park secondary tasks.
• Mute alerts; clear visual clutter.
• Close extra tabs; take a short break.

title: MEASURE THE EMOTION’S VELOCITY
goal: Track whether an emotion is rising, steady, or falling before acting from its intensity.
steps:
1. Set Level — At three intervals, keep not only level but direction and speed: rising fast, steady, falling slowly.
2. Add Action — Add the action impulse at each point.
3. Make Decisions — Make decisions from trajectory plus facts, not from the first intensity number alone.
win: Three readings showed level, direction, speed, and action urge, so the decision used the whole trajectory.
supports:
• Make access harder; use your hands.
• Tell someone if the urge spikes; change rooms if possible.
• Keep your hands busy; remember urges peak and fall.
• Change locations; avoid bargaining.
• Avoid bargaining with the urge; delay ten minutes.
formula_flow: Set Level → Add Action → Make Decisions
safety:
PAUSE
Escalating risk calls for support before further tracking.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: HALF-SPEED THE FIRST MOVE
goal: Slow only the first urge-linked movement and decide whether the next movement should happen.
steps:
1. Identify Earliest — Catch the first movement linked to the urge—turning, reaching, standing, typing.
2. Observe Direction — Do only that movement at half speed while observing its direction and tension.
3. Pause Completion — Pause at completion and decide whether the second movement serves you.
win: The initial reach, turn, stand, or type finished at half speed and ended in a fresh choice point.
supports:
• Make access harder; remember urges peak and fall.
• Drink some water; make access less convenient.
• Do one incompatible activity; move away from the cue.
• Tell someone early; delay acting for ten minutes.
• Leave the trigger; change locations.
formula_flow: Identify Earliest → Observe Direction → Pause Completion
safety:
PAUSE
Do not slow a movement needed for immediate safety.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RETURN EACH LOAD TO ITS SOURCE
goal: Give each source of stress only the share of body alarm it actually contributed.
steps:
1. Estimate Contribution — Name current stressors and estimate each contribution to body alarm.
2. Imagine Arrows — Imagine arrows from the present feeling back to its actual sources.
3. Stop Blaming — Address the largest actionable contributor first; stop blaming the most visible issue for unrelated load.
win: The largest actionable source became clearer, and the most visible problem stopped carrying unrelated load.
supports:
• Seek care for new severe symptoms; unclench your jaw.
• Reduce caffeine; let breathing stay natural.
• Wait out the surge; use ordinary surroundings.
• Sip water if it helps; avoid repeated pulse checking.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; keep your body supported.

safety:

title: THE EMOTION STOPS AT THE SKIN
goal: Keep another person's emotion on their side of the boundary while choosing what help is truly yours.
steps:
1. Emotion — Notice where their emotion seems to enter your body.
2. Trace Physical — Trace your physical boundary with gaze or touch.
3. State Action — State what action is yours, what remains theirs, and what you can offer without taking ownership.
4. Stay Blurred — Adjust distance if the distinction stays blurred.
win: Their feeling, your action, and the support you could offer stayed distinct enough to adjust distance if needed.
supports:
• Leave their reaction with them; take time before saying yes.
• Protect your capacity; use one clear sentence.
• Notice resentment as a warning; repeat the same wording calmly.
• Offer only genuine options; let guilt pass.
• Notice resentment early; decide your limit before answering.

safety:
PAUSE
Honour mandated or genuine care responsibilities rather than withdrawing reflexively.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MATCH THE PRESSURE, THEN ZERO IT
goal: Match two sides of physical pressure, then lower both together back to zero.
steps:
1. Press Equal — Press palms together—or both hands into one cushion—at about twenty percent effort. Keep breathing ordinary.
2. Match Force — Adjust until neither side wins and the pressure feels equal. Hold that match for two seconds.
3. Step Down — Lower both sides together through three gentle levels: fifteen, ten, then five percent.
4. Reach Zero — Reach zero, rest both hands on a stable surface, and observe whether the urge to press returns.
win: Equal resistance stepped down through lighter levels until your hands rested and the urge to press could be checked.
supports:

• Remember urges peak and fall; avoid bargaining with the urge.
• Ride the peak; use your hands.
• Make access less convenient; move away from the cue.
• Delay acting for ten minutes; make access harder.

title: PIN A RETURN ADDRESS
goal: Leave yourself an exact restart point instead of rescanning the whole task later.
steps:
1. Name Task — Name the exact task currently carrying your attention.
2. Locate — Name the precise place inside it where you stopped.
3. Choose Verb — Choose one next verb: compare, type, turn, check, send, or place.
4. Re-enter — Repeat task, location, verb once and act without rescanning everything.
win: Task, stopping place, and next verb were remembered once and used to resume directly.
supports:
• Close extra tabs; use one screen.
• Silence nonessential notifications; mute alerts.
• Clear visual clutter; park secondary tasks.
• Protect one focus block; reduce background noise.
• Finish or park one open loop; choose one target.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not rely on a return address for driving, medication, machinery, clinical procedures, or tasks requiring a complete safety recheck.

title: DISASSEMBLE THE ALARM PANEL
goal: Change only the quietest safe channel of body alarm and leave the louder ones alone.
steps:
1. Read Channels — Read three channels without searching your whole body: SPEED, PRESSURE, and TEMPERATURE. Use lower, medium, or high.
2. Pick Smallest — Choose the safest channel with the lowest intensity. Do not pick the loudest one.
3. Move Dial — Move only that channel one step: slow one hand movement, soften one contact point, or adjust one safe layer of warmth or coolness.
4. Check Panel — Check whether that channel changed at all. Let the other two channels remain exactly as they are.
win: Speed, pressure, and temperature were read separately, then one lower-intensity channel moved a single step.
supports:
• Wait out the surge; reduce extra stimulation.
• Unclench your jaw; sit somewhere safe.
• Avoid symptom searching; use ordinary surroundings.
• Loosen your shoulders; stop body scanning.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; sip water if it helps.
formula_flow: Read Channels → Pick Smallest → Move Dial → Check Panel
safety:
PAUSE
New, severe, or unusual physical symptoms require medical assessment. Stop for pain, faintness, breathing difficulty, confusion, or loss of orientation.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

2. Choose Opposite — Choose an opposite rhythm: agitated becomes deliberate, collapsed becomes lightly brisk, looping becomes irregular.
3. Observe Emotional — Maintain the new tempo through one simple task and observe the emotional shift.

WIN
One simple task was completed at a deliberately different rhythm, producing fresh information about the state.

• Wait before sending messages; lower stimulation for a minute.
• Slow physical pace; name the emotion.
• Delay the message; notice what changed physically.
• Do one steadying action; let intensity fall.
• Check the facts separately; rest before deciding.

MIND BEND
Emotion is partly carried in tempo. Changing cadence can alter what the body predicts before the story changes.

FORMULA FLOW
Cadence → Choose Opposite → Observe Emotional

SAFETY
PAUSE
Match movement to medical ability and avoid breath manipulation if activating.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: OPEN THE IDENTITY PORTFOLIO
goal: Give one neglected identity a small real action instead of letting one role consume the week.
steps:
1. Estimate Much — Name five identities active in your life and estimate how much attention each received this week.
2. Choose Neglected — Choose the neglected role that still matters.
3. Use Another Share — Do one tiny action from its perspective today—friend, learner, neighbour, artist, caregiver, citizen.
win: A role that mattered but had received little attention got one concrete vote today.
supports:
• Return to one target; mute alerts.
• Use a short focus block; close extra tabs.
• Silence nonessential notifications; reduce nearby noise.
• Finish or park one open loop; clear visual clutter.
• Use one screen; close what you do not need.
formula_flow: Estimate Much → Choose Neglected → Use Another Share
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use role expansion to avoid urgent responsibilities in the dominant role.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: GLOBAL LABELS NEED THREE RECEIPTS
goal: Test a global identity label against recent evidence that both supports and complicates it.
steps:
1. Name Appears — When a global label appears, name three recent behaviours that support it and three that complicate it.
2. Replace Identity — If the evidence is mixed, replace identity with a narrower situational description.
win: Six behaviours made the label narrower, or showed that a situational description fit better.
supports:
• Add the missing context; question absolute words.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; look for one missing fact.
• Ask what else could fit; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Separate guess from evidence; check what you actually know.
• Check another angle; notice absolute words like always.
formula_flow: Name Appears → Replace Identity
safety:
PAUSE
Do not turn the audit into exhaustive self-surveillance.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ADD THE TEMPORARY CLAUSE
goal: Add the conditions and time limit that a harsh self-judgment leaves out.
steps:
1. State Conditions — Append this qualifier to the self-judgement: ‘in this state, under these conditions, for now.’ Name the state and conditions precisely.
2. Identify Condition — Then spot one condition likely to change and one action that could influence it.
win: The verdict became temporary and specific enough to reveal one condition that could actually change.
supports:
• Use two minutes; open only what you need.
• Open the task; use one window.
• Lower standards briefly; use a visible cue.
• Touch the first item; begin with the easiest part.
• Do the easiest useful part; make it visible.
formula_flow: State Conditions → Identify Condition
safety:
PAUSE
Seek assessment when a serious or persistent condition needs care.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE PRICE OF KEEPING THIS SELF
goal: Measure what a self-concept permits, blocks, and demands before deciding whether it still serves you.
steps:
1. Sort Identity Costs — Imagine three buckets: IT LETS ME; IT STOPS ME; IT DEMANDS FROM ME.
2. Fill The Buckets — Mentally sort the self-concept into those three buckets.
3. Find The Price — Focus on the highest hidden cost and ask whether the identity still earns its keep.
win: The hidden cost became visible enough to question whether keeping the identity was worth its price.
supports:
• Cut the task; make the first move tiny.
• Set a two-minute timer; shrink the first action.
• Reward starting, not finishing; lower the first demand.
• Open the task; do the easiest useful part.
• Remove one barrier; skip extra setup.

safety:
PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: PRACTISE THE QUALITY ANONYMOUSLY
goal: Practise one unfamiliar positive quality privately before deciding whether it is 'you'.
steps:
1. Choose Positive — Choose a positive quality that feels “not me.” Do one behaviour that expresses it without announcing the quality or claiming a new identity.
2. Ask Brave — Ask the brave question, make the playful move, accept the compliment, or offer the clear boundary.
3. Let Proof Arrive — Let evidence arrive before identity approval.
win: The behaviour happened without announcing a new identity, letting evidence arrive before self-definition.
supports:
• Do not debate your limit; let guilt pass.
• Delay your answer; decide your limit before answering.
• Repeat without arguing; offer only genuine options.
• Leave their reaction with them; keep the limit simple.
• Leave reactions with them; do not overexplain the limit.

title: REMOVE THE AUDIENCE
goal: Remove the imagined audience and choose from direct consequences plus values.
steps:
1. Imagine Nobody — Imagine nobody will see, praise, criticise, repost, or hear about the action.
2. Erase Audience — Erase the imagined audience one row at a time.
3. Choose Direct — What would you choose if only direct consequences and values remained.
4. Take Smallest — Take the smallest version privately.
win: Praise, criticism, reposts, and reputation disappeared from the decision, leaving one private action you still wanted.
supports:
• Use one priority; make the next hour reflect it.
• Act before motivation; check whose goal you are chasing.
• Check whose goal; pick one value for this decision.
• Keep meaning practical; remove one conflicting commitment.
• Review what the action costs; use values to choose trade-offs.

title: CALL THE INNER COUNCIL
goal: Let different inner needs speak once, then give coordination to the part protecting the whole system.
steps:
1. Give Self — Give each self-state an imagined place.
2. Sentence — One sentence each: what I need, what I fear, what I propose.
3. Protect Whole — Appoint an inner coordinator whose job is to protect the whole system over time.
4. Guide Council — Let that coordinator combine, delay, or reject proposals while acknowledging every need.
win: Each self-state was heard without becoming the chairperson, and one coordinator decided what could combine, wait, or be declined.
supports:
• Lower the quality bar; choose tiny action.
• Prepare the task in advance; lower standards briefly.
• Lower the first demand; do the easiest useful part.
• Choose a rough beginning; begin while unsure.
• Use one window; enter through easy work.

safety:
PAUSE
Use professional support if parts feel autonomous, dangerous, or disorganising.

title: EXIST FOR ONE MINUTE WITHOUT AUTOBIOGRAPHY
goal: Spend one minute in direct experience without using your biography to explain who is here.
steps:
1. Don't Recall — For sixty seconds, do not recall name, history, status, or plans.
2. Stay Changing — Stay with changing sound, pressure, light, and movement.
3. Simple — Notice the simple ongoing sense of being present through those changes.
4. End Reclaim — Reclaim your biography on purpose at the end.
win: Sound, pressure, light, and movement continued while name, status, history, and plans stayed temporarily offline.
supports:
• Separate possibility from probability; delay the verdict.
• Question absolute words; check another angle.
• Use a real example; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Separate guess from evidence; use current facts.
• Ask what would disprove it; check what you actually know.
formula_flow: Don't Recall → Stay Changing → Simple → End Reclaim
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if life-story quiet creates feeling unreal or detached from yourself.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MOVE THE MEMORY CAMERA
goal: Change the camera position of a memory while keeping the events themselves accurate.
steps:
1. Place Memory — Place the memory on a screen with enough visual distance.
2. View Scene — View the scene from above, behind, or beside a compassionate observer.
3. Keep Events — Keep events accurate while changing camera position.
4. Add Resources — Add current-you outside the frame with present resources.
win: The scene was seen from a different distance or angle, with current-you and present resources outside the old frame.
supports:
• Replace one response; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Keep replacement easy; reset without self-criticism.
• Interrupt the usual sequence; move the cue.
• Change the environment; notice the first automatic moment.
• Make the new habit easier; add small friction.
formula_flow: Place Memory → View Scene → Keep Events → Add Resources
safety:
PAUSE
Traumatic memory perspective work should be supported if destabilising.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE MEMORY DOES NOT END THERE
goal: Restore what came after the painful ending instead of letting memory stop at the worst frame.
steps:
1. End Retell — Retell only enough to reach the painful ending.
2. Follow Escape — Then append what actually followed: escape, help, adaptation, learning, regained ability, or today’s status.
3. Don't Invent — Do not invent redemption.
4. Restore — Restore the omitted chronology.
win: The chronology continued into real help, adaptation, learning, regained ability, or today's status without invented redemption.
supports:
• Reduce easy access to triggers; change one cue.
• Notice the first automatic moment; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Reset after slips; keep replacement easy.
• Notice the trigger; make the new habit easier.
• Change the environment; interrupt the sequence.
formula_flow: End Retell → Follow Escape → Don't Invent → Restore
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid forced positive meaning where aftermath remains unresolved.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: POWER THEN, RESOURCES NOW

steps:

• Set a two-minute timer; restart quickly.
• Begin with the easiest part; skip extra setup.

title: SAY THE SENTENCE HISTORY NEVER RECEIVED
goal: Say the words the past never received while making clear that today cannot rewrite then.
steps:
1. Picture Words — Picture the exact words you could not say or hear.
2. Speak Empty — Say them quietly in your mind or to an empty room while clearly stating that this is present-day completion, not a changed past.
3. Add Response — Add the response current-you can now provide.
win: The missing sentence was expressed and current-you supplied a response without pretending history had changed.
supports:
• Lower the first demand; begin with the easiest part.
• Begin while unsure; remove one barrier.
• Choose tiny action; set a two-minute timer.
• Start before you feel ready; lower standards briefly.
• Skip extra setup; use one window.

SAY THE SENTENCE HISTORY NEVER RECEIVED

PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Say the words the past never received while making clear that today cannot rewrite then.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Picture Words — Picture the exact words you could not say or hear.

3. Add Response — Add the response current-you can now provide.

WIN
The missing sentence was expressed and current-you supplied a response without pretending history had changed.

• Lower the first demand; begin with the easiest part.
• Begin while unsure; remove one barrier.
• Choose tiny action; set a two-minute timer.
• Start before you feel ready; lower standards briefly.
• Skip extra setup; use one window.

Completion can happen now without rewriting the past. An unsaid truth may still need somewhere to land.

Picture Words → Speak Empty → Add Response

PAUSE

This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ADD THE WITNESS WHO SHOULD HAVE BEEN THERE
goal: Add the protective witness who should have named what was wrong and what you deserved.
steps:
1. Introduce — Introduce a compassionate observer appropriate to the event—a trusted adult, advocate, elder, clinician, or current-you.
2. Name Wrong — Have them name what was wrong, what protection was deserved, and what is true about the person who endured it.
3. Keep It Believable — Keep their words believable.
win: A believable observer supplied protection, truth, and context that the original scene had lacked.
supports:
• Keep one real task in view; reduce commentary.
• Let the thought stay unfinished; avoid building a larger story.
• Drop the need to solve it; let it pass.
• Use fewer words about it; keep one task.
• Notice the thought, then step back; stop debating.
formula_flow: Introduce → Name Wrong → Keep It Believable
safety:
PAUSE
Use guided trauma work if imagined witnessing intensifies grief or flashback.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ASK WHAT THE MEMORY IS STILL BILLING
goal: Find what a memory is still demanding and route that demand to the right present response.
steps:
1. Headline Event — State the event as one factual headline with no motive and without rebuilding sensory details.
2. Extract Claim — Finish this sentence once: ‘This memory still seems to demand ___.’ Keep only one claim.
3. Route Bill — Route the claim to BOUNDARY, REPAIR, GRIEF, or IMPOSSIBLE REVERSAL. Do not create a fifth category.
4. Act Present — Choose the matching present response: set protection, request safe repair, make room for grief, or stop billing today for a reversal history cannot provide.
win: The claim became boundary, repair, grief, or impossible reversal, and the next action matched that category.
supports:
• Return to current task; use a short timer.
• Set a stop time; leave unsolved questions.
• Shift attention outward; limit how long you review it.
• Change rooms; name one useful action.
• Set a clear stopping point; use your hands.
formula_flow: Headline Event → Extract Claim → Route Bill → Act Present
safety:
PAUSE
Do not contact unsafe people, seek revenge, force reconciliation, or use this game during trauma flooding or immediate danger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SAVE THE LESSON, DELETE THE VERDICT
goal: Keep the specific lesson from a painful event without letting it become a verdict on your whole life.
steps:
1. Save Lesson — Name the specific lesson the event genuinely supports.
2. Spot Verdict — Notice the global conclusion attached to it: ‘Nobody is safe,’ ‘I am weak,’ ‘Life is over,’ or another all-life verdict.
3. Separate Them — Ask whether the specific lesson still works without the global verdict. Keep what teaches; delete what condemns.
win: A useful lesson survived after the global condemnation was removed.
supports:
• Look for one missing fact; separate guess from evidence.
• Use current facts; delay major conclusions when upset.
• Question absolute words; test the assumption.
• Use a real example; check what you actually know.
• Ask what else could fit; notice absolute words like always.
formula_flow: Save Lesson → Spot Verdict → Separate Them
safety:
PAUSE
Do not dilute lessons that accurately identify continuing danger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ENTER THROUGH A RANDOM DOOR
goal: Let a random workable section choose the starting point when order does not matter.
steps:
1. Number Doors — Name three to six task sections that can safely be done in any order and give each one a number.

3. Enter There — Work only inside that section for ninety seconds; do not reorganise the whole project.
4. Mark Progress — Notice one concrete sign of progress, then decide whether to choose another number or close.
win: Ninety seconds of real progress happened inside one section without reorganising the whole project first.
supports:
• Touch the first item; cut the task.
• Enter through easy work; do the easiest useful part.
• Start before you feel ready; prepare the task in advance.
• Restart quickly; open only what you need.
• Use two minutes; shrink the first action.

title: SET UP WHILE ENERGY IS CHEAP
goal: Use a higher-energy moment to prepare the task for a lower-energy one.
steps:
1. Prepare Requirement — During a higher-energy window, prepare everything the task will need: pack it, charge it, open it, measure it, place it, or prefill it.
2. Leave Final — Leave only the final movement for the difficult time.
3. Leave It Ready — Picture the setup in its ready state.
win: Materials, access, or setup were ready in advance, leaving only the final starting movement for later.
supports:
• Start before you feel ready; use two minutes.
• Reward starting, not finishing; touch the first item.
• Make the first move tiny; skip extra setup.
• Stop planning after one action; do the easiest useful part.
• Choose tiny action; start with one minute.

PAUSE

title: LEAVE A BRIDGE BACK
goal: Leave the future version of you one exact phrase that points back into the task.
steps:
1. Stop Precise — Before stopping, picture the exact next movement and current reasoning.
2. Mark Re-entry — Hold one short phrase that tells you where to resume.
3. Leave Cleanly — End the task without mentally reopening the whole plan.
4. Return — On return, use the phrase and continue from that exact point.
win: The task ended with the next movement and reasoning preserved, so return did not require reopening the whole plan.
supports:
• Stop planning after one action; choose a rough beginning.
• Set a two-minute timer; make it visible.
• Start with one minute; remove one barrier.
• Begin while unsure; use one window.
• Prepare the task in advance; restart quickly.
formula_flow: Stop Precise → Mark Re-entry → Leave Cleanly → Return
safety:
PAUSE
Update the bridge when conditions or priorities change.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

ritualText:
LEAVE A BRIDGE BACK

PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Leave the future version of you one exact phrase that points back into the task.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Stop Precise — Before stopping, picture the exact next movement and current reasoning.
2. Mark Re-entry — Hold one short phrase that tells you where to resume.
3. Leave Cleanly — End the task without mentally reopening the whole plan.
4. Return — On return, use the phrase and continue from that exact point.

WIN
The task ended with the next movement and reasoning preserved, so return did not require reopening the whole plan.

• Stop planning after one action; choose a rough beginning.
• Set a two-minute timer; make it visible.
• Start with one minute; remove one barrier.
• Begin while unsure; use one window.
• Prepare the task in advance; restart quickly.

MIND BEND
Stopping is less costly when context is intentionally cached. A bridge back prevents tomorrow from paying today's setup cost again.

FORMULA FLOW
Stop Precise → Mark Re-entry → Leave Cleanly → Return

SAFETY
PAUSE
Update the bridge when conditions or priorities change.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

• Lower the first demand; begin while unsure.

title: THE VERSION THAT STILL COUNTS
goal: Finish the smallest version that still serves the task's essential purpose.
steps:
1. Name Task — Name the task’s essential purpose.
2. Remove Feature — Remove every feature not required for that purpose.
3. Build Smallest — Build the smallest deliverable that still works, submit or finish it, then upgrade only if time and value justify the addition.
win: Nonessential features were removed and a usable deliverable existed before any optional upgrade.
supports:
• Ship useful work; ask what is actually required.
• Leave minor flaws alone; limit checking passes.
• Follow the brief; set finish time.
• Stop low-value changes; limit checking.
• Separate important errors from polish; define good enough first.
formula_flow: Name Task → Remove Feature → Build Smallest
safety:
PAUSE
Maintain full standards for safety-critical, clinical, legal, or hard to undo work.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

win: The desired cue became the easiest thing to notice and immediately linked to the first action.

title: THE LAPSE FIRE DRILL
goal: Prepare the exact recovery sequence for the first lapse before a second lapse can be negotiated.
steps:
1. Name What Happened — Pre-plan three actions after a lapse: name what happened without judgement; restore the environment or schedule; do the next smallest valid repetition.
2. Store — Store the script beside the behaviour.
3. Use After — Use it after one miss—before a second is negotiated.
win: One miss triggered naming, restoration, and the next valid repetition without a character judgment.
supports:
• Stop checking their numbers; name one thing already working.
• Track progress by your values; notice what you cannot see.
• Limit social media exposure; avoid one-person benchmarks.
• Compare with your past self; use your own priorities.
• Keep context visible; return to your priorities.
formula_flow: Name What Happened → Store → Use After
safety:
PAUSE
Escalate to support when lapses involve danger, relapse, or repeated loss of control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SET THE LIMIT BEFORE THE NEXT TEST
goal: Define the boundary in camera-visible terms and decide the consequence before the next test.
steps:
1. Count Pattern — Define the behaviour in terms a camera could observe.
2. Set Threshold — Choose the count, duration, or date that marks the limit.
3. Link Consequence — Choose one consequence under your control, such as ending the call, leaving, or changing access.
4. Follow Contract — If the threshold is crossed, follow the contract once without debating motive.
win: A clear threshold and an action under your control were ready to execute without debating motive.
supports:
• Notice resentment early; repeat without arguing.
• Decide your limit before answering; offer only genuine options.
• Use a short no; offer alternatives only if genuine.
• Let guilt pass; state consequences clearly.
• Protect your capacity; notice resentment as a warning.
formula_flow: Count Pattern → Set Threshold → Link Consequence → Follow Contract
safety:
PAUSE
Leave immediately instead of counting repetitions when there is intimidation, violence, or immediate danger.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: RELATIONSHIP DATA, NOT ONE BIG FEELING
goal: Review a relationship as separate events, frequency, context, repair, and outcomes.
steps:
1. Hold Event — Keep the event, context, frequency, repair attempt, and outcome as separate mental snapshots. Feel the surface supporting you.
2. Look Repetition — Look for repetition and exceptions.
3. Issue Narrow — Make a narrow conclusion about the observed period instead of using ‘always’ or ‘never’.
win: Patterns and exceptions both stayed visible, producing a narrow conclusion instead of 'always' or 'never'.
supports:
• Ask what else could fit; check another angle.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; question absolute words.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; delay the verdict.
• Separate guess from evidence; check the base rate.
• Check the whole situation; test the assumption.
formula_flow: Hold Event → Look Repetition → Issue Narrow
safety:
PAUSE
Do not use data collection to remain in an unsafe relationship.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TURN DOWN ONE DOOR, NOT THE WHOLE HOUSE
goal: Reduce exactly one kind of access without shutting down the entire relationship.
steps:
1. Name Contact — Name the contact pattern you want to change without judging the person.
2. Pick Door — Choose exactly one access door: TIME, TOPIC, CHANNEL, LOCATION, or FREQUENCY.
3. Lower One — Lower that door by one clear level: shorter call, one topic excluded, text only, public place, or fewer contacts.
4. Hold Setting — State the new setting and leave every other door unchanged for this round.
win: Time, topic, channel, location, or frequency changed by one level while the other doors remained untouched.
supports:
• Keep consequences realistic; do not overexplain the limit.
• Repeat without arguing; take time before saying yes.
• Notice resentment as a warning; do not debate your limit.
• Repeat the same wording calmly; offer alternatives only if genuine.
• Delay your answer; offer only genuine options.
formula_flow: Name Contact → Pick Door → Lower One → Hold Setting
safety:
PAUSE
If there is abuse, stalking, coercion, violence, or immediate danger, prioritise safety planning and professional support over gradual access changes.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: UNDERSTAND, THEN DISAGREE CLEANLY
goal: Understand the other view accurately, then place your disagreement in its own sentence.
steps:
1. View They — Summarise their view until they could recognise it.
2. Name Need — Name the need or logic you understand.
3. Say Meaning — Then say exactly where your meaning, value, or decision differs.
4. Receive Own — No ‘but’ inside the summary; disagreement receives its own sentence.
win: Their position was recognisable before your different meaning, value, or decision was stated.
supports:
• Change one cue; interrupt the usual sequence.
• Reset after slips; make the new habit easier.
• Notice the first automatic moment; delay the routine.
• Add small friction; replace one response.
• Change the environment; make the old habit harder.

safety:

title: APOLOGY NEEDS THREE EVIDENCE POINTS
goal: Judge an apology by acknowledgement, changed action, and prevention evidence over time.
steps:
1. Return Define — Define what adequate repair requires: clear acknowledgement, changed action, and prevention of return.
2. Specify — Specify what evidence would show each over time.
3. Evaluate — Check the apology against those criteria rather than immediate emotion.
win: Repair was measured against three observable criteria rather than the emotion of the moment.
supports:
• Wait before sending messages; give the feeling time to move.
• Let intensity fall; rest before deciding.
• Use simple words for the problem; delay the message.
• Separate feeling from fact; notice body tension.
• Do one steadying action; check the facts separately.
formula_flow: Return Define → Specify → Evaluate
safety:
PAUSE
No repair test obliges renewed contact after serious harm.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: MAP THE RELATIONSHIP LABOUR
goal: Measure who carries the hidden work of the relationship across a defined period.
steps:
1. Plan Carries — Across a defined period, tally who initiates, accommodates, repairs, plans, and carries emotional follow-up.

win: Initiation, accommodation, repair, planning, and follow-up became categories that could support one concrete rebalance request.
supports:
• Avoid treating guesses as facts; test the assumption.
• Ask what would change your mind; delay the verdict.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; notice absolute words like always.
• Separate possibility from probability; ask what else could fit.
• Check another angle; look for one missing fact.

safety:
PAUSE
Do not use the map to demand identical contributions under unequal circumstances.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ASK THE QUESTION FEAR KEEPS ANSWERING
goal: Ask the question that could genuinely prove your assumption wrong.
steps:
1. Picture Assumption — Picture the assumption driving your reaction.
2. Question Whose — Convert it into one clear, non-leading question whose answer could prove the assumption wrong.
3. Ask Suitable — Ask at a suitable time, listen fully, and compare reply plus later behaviour with the original model.
win: A non-leading question replaced the feared answer, and the reply plus later behaviour could update the original model.
supports:
• Use one concrete example; check the request.
• Use shorter sentences when tense; end with action.
• Use one example; confirm the owner.
• Separate facts from tone; ask for a specific next action.
• Keep one issue per conversation; lead with the point.

safety:
PAUSE

title: POSTURE WITHOUT PROPHECY
goal: Use a stable open posture without treating posture as a prediction about the outcome.
steps:
1. Adopt — Take a stable, non-defensive position: feet supported, spine available, gaze level, arms unguarded enough for safety.
2. Refuse Prophecy — Do not use the posture to predict success or failure.
3. Hold for Evidence — Keep the posture while you wait for actual evidence.
win: Your body stayed supported and non-defensive while actual evidence, not pose, decided what the situation meant.
supports:
• Reduce extra stimulation; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Avoid repeated pulse checking; keep movements gentle.
• Sit somewhere safe; let breaths happen.
• Unclench your jaw; seek care for new severe symptoms.
• Sip water if it helps; stop body scanning.
formula_flow: Adopt → Refuse Prophecy → Hold for Evidence
safety:

title: CHOOSE THE EASIEST MISTAKE TO CATCH
goal: Prefer the option whose failure becomes visible while correction is still practical.
steps:
1. Name Options — Name the two or three live options. For each, picture the specific way it could fail—not a vague fear.
2. Name Failure — Name the earliest visible sign that failure has begun. It must be visible or clear, not a feeling alone.
3. Warning — State what corrective action would still be available when that sign appears and what cost has already accumulated.
4. Choose Visible — Choose the option whose reliable warning arrives while correction is still practical. Use this as one decision criterion, not the whole verdict.
win: Each option had a specific failure sign, remaining correction, and accumulated cost before one warning system was favoured.
supports:
• Delay the message; lower stimulation for a minute.
• Do one steadying action; name the emotion.
• Wait before sending messages; use simple words for the problem.
• Lower nearby noise; use plain language.
• Rest before deciding; notice what changed physically.

ritualText:
TAKE UP 5% MORE SPACE

PLAY TIME
45–60 seconds

GOAL
Expand your posture slightly and notice which words become easier to access.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Widen Feet — Widen feet, elbows, chest, or seating position by a small manageable amount.
2. Keep Change — Keep the change below performance or dominance.
3. Observe Shape — Observe what the expanded shape signals internally and which words become easier to access.

WIN
A small increase in physical space changed the internal signal without becoming dominance or performance.

• Lower stimulation for a minute; rest before deciding.
• Wait before sending messages; eat, drink, or rest if needed.
• Check the facts separately; slow physical pace.
• Check basic needs; use simple words for the problem.
• Give the feeling time to move; notice body tension.

MIND BEND
Posture can constrain language; taking a little more space may make options available that felt inaccessible in a collapsed shape.

FORMULA FLOW
Widen Feet → Keep Change → Observe Shape

SAFETY
PAUSE
Stay compact when wider posture would make the situation less safe.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: UNWIND IN REVERSE
goal: Release a tension chain in the reverse order that it built.
steps:
1. Recall Muscle — Recall which muscle group tightened last.
2. Soften Work — Soften it first, then work back toward the first area that braced.
3. Pause Handoff — Pause between groups to feel the handoff.
4. Finish Original — Finish at the original starting point and compare the whole chain.
win: Each muscle group handed the release onward until you could compare the original bracing point with its starting state.
supports:
• Unclench your jaw and shoulders; keep your body supported.
• Avoid symptom searching; reduce extra stimulation.
• Let breaths happen; keep movements gentle.
• Sit somewhere safe; reduce caffeine.
• Wait out the surge; stop body scanning.
formula_flow: Recall Muscle → Soften Work → Pause Handoff → Finish Original
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid manipulating painful, injured, or medically affected areas.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHICH WAY DOES THE URGE POINT?
goal: Read the direction of an urge before deciding how to respond to it.
steps:
1. Act Classify — Without acting, classify the bodily impulse as toward, away, against, downward, upward, or still.
2. Body — Notice the body region carrying the arrow.
3. Ask Safe — Ask what safe action could honour the information without blindly completing the vector.
win: Toward, away, against, down, up, or still became clear without the movement being automatically completed.
supports:
• Avoid symptom searching; let breathing stay natural.
• Let breaths happen; sip water if it helps.
• Sit somewhere safe; keep movements gentle.
• Use ordinary surroundings; reduce extra stimulation.
• Look at ordinary objects nearby; stay somewhere physically safe.

• Avoid symptom searching; let breathing stay natural.

title: FINISH THE BODY'S FULL STOP
goal: Complete one safe defensive movement slowly, then return all effort to zero.
steps:

• Make access harder; delay ten minutes.
• Eat or drink if hunger matters; tell someone early.

title: BORROW STILLNESS FROM THE WALL
goal: Use an imagined stable line as a reference without forcing your inner state to copy it.
steps:
1. Imagine Still Line — Picture a stable horizontal line or horizon.
2. Compare — Notice its imagined stillness beside the movement inside your body and mind.
3. Allow Both — Do not force inner movement to match the line.
4. Borrow Stability — Let the stable image become a reference for one slow breath.
win: Movement inside could continue while one slow breath borrowed orientation from something pictured as still.
supports:
• Name today's date; look around slowly.
• Keep eyes open; return to one real sound.
• Look around the room; notice where your body is supported.
• Reduce sensory input if needed; track one texture.
• Notice three colours; feel the chair.
formula_flow: Imagine Still Line → Compare → Allow Both → Borrow Stability
safety:
PAUSE
Do not stare at one point when operating a vehicle or feeling dizzy.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: SORT THE SOUNDS BY DISTANCE
goal: Use near, middle, and far sounds to reopen the sense of space around you.
steps:
1. Identify Nearest — Spot the nearest sound, one mid-distance sound, and the farthest audible layer.
2. Move Attention — Move attention outward through those distances, then back once.
3. Let Far — Let the far sound widen the perceived space around the closest one.
win: Attention travelled outward and back once, and the farthest sound made the nearest layer feel less enclosing.
supports:
• Keep new facts separate; stop researching after enough evidence.
• Set a decision deadline; avoid reopening without new facts.
• Ignore imagined regret; limit the options.
• Choose the option you can support; name the non-negotiables.
• Stop extra research; choose by the strongest evidence.
formula_flow: Identify Nearest → Move Attention → Let Far
safety:
PAUSE
Use hearing protection rather than attention practice in unsafe noise.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

2. Explore — Notice pressure, warmth, ridges, resistance, and tiny changes.
3. Name Detail — Name three details that require fresh sensory attention.

• Name one useful action; end the replay.
• Shift attention outward; name one action.
• Change rooms; ask for new information.
• Stop solving the unsolvable; set a clear stopping point.
• Change rooms if possible; ask if any new information exists.

title: LET ONE TASTE FINISH

2. Track Taste — Track taste from first contact through peak, transformation, and complete disappearance.

win: Flavour moved from first contact through peak and disappearance, revealing when wanting continued after tasting ended.

• Return to one real sound; feel both feet.
• Name three visible objects; feel the chair.

title: THE ROOM HAS JOBS, NOT DEMANDS
goal: Keep only the room function that supports the next safe action and dismiss the rest for now.
steps:
1. Imagine Four Things — Picture four ordinary things from a familiar room.
2. Name Jobs — Give each only its basic job: support, light, hold, open.
3. Drop Demands — Say NOT NEEDED NOW to every function irrelevant to this moment.
4. Choose Helper — Keep only the imagined function that supports your next safe action.
win: Ordinary objects returned to simple jobs, leaving one useful function active instead of a room full of demands.
supports:
• Start with one minute; begin with the easiest part.
• Start smaller; use one window.
• Use two minutes; remove one barrier.
• Shrink the first action; set a two-minute timer.
• Remove one obvious distraction; choose a rough beginning.
formula_flow: Imagine Four Things → Name Jobs → Drop Demands → Choose Helper
safety:
PAUSE
Stop for visual pain, dizziness, nausea, disorientation, compulsive scanning, or any real emergency requiring immediate action.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: TRANSLATE ACROSS SENSES
goal: Translate a feeling or sensation into another sensory form, then change one feature.
steps:
1. Represent — Represent tension as a texture, a sound as a shape, or an emotion as colour and movement.
2. Make Translation — Make the translation concrete enough to picture or gesture.
3. Observe Whether — Alter one property in the new medium and observe whether the first state changes.
win: Texture, shape, colour, sound, or movement shifted and revealed whether the original state changed with it.
supports:
• Reduce sensory input if needed; name three visible objects.
• Name today's date; feel the chair.
• Notice three colours; return to one real sound.
• Touch a stable surface; look around slowly.
• Track one texture; keep your eyes on something steady.
formula_flow: Represent → Make Translation → Observe Whether
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if cross-sensory imagery becomes confusing or perceptually disturbing.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: COUNT EVERY OPEN LOOP
goal: Count every unresolved mental loop without trying to solve any of them yet.
steps:
1. Question Task — Name every unresolved promise, question, task, decision, and waiting item without solving any.
2. Use Line — Use one line each.
3. Imagine Boundary — When nothing else appears for thirty seconds, imagine a boundary around the inventory and choose a separate processing time.
win: Promises, tasks, questions, decisions, and waiting items became a bounded inventory with a later processing time.
supports:
• Close what you do not need; silence nonessential notifications.
• Keep one task visible; park secondary tasks.
• Close extra tabs; use a short focus block.
• Mute alerts; return after interruptions.
• Protect one focus block; choose one target.
formula_flow: Question Task → Use Line → Imagine Boundary
safety:
PAUSE
End the capture if list-making increases overwhelm without containment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: ONE ACTIVE SLOT
goal: Protect one active concern while giving the next item and the rest clear places to wait.
steps:
1. Create Positions — Create three positions: ACTIVE, WAITING, ARCHIVE.
2. Wait Route — Put only one concern in ACTIVE, one likely next item in WAITING, and mentally route everything else to ARCHIVE with a clear retrieval cue.
3. Give Active — Give the active concern a protected time box.
win: One concern occupied ACTIVE, one sat in WAITING, and everything else had a retrieval cue in ARCHIVE.
supports:
• Return to one target; keep one task visible.
• Reduce nearby noise; put the phone out of reach.
• Return after interruptions; protect one focus block.
• Park secondary tasks; close what you do not need.
• Use one screen; choose one target.
formula_flow: Create Positions → Wait Route → Give Active
safety:
PAUSE
Expand active capacity only when parallel monitoring is genuinely required.

title: HIDE THE OPTION NAMES
goal: Compare options on relevant traits before reconnecting them to their emotionally loaded names.
steps:
1. Rename Options — In your mind, rename the leading options A, B, and C.
2. Choose Traits — Pick three relevant traits such as time, fit, reliability, or learning.
3. Rank Traits — Compare A, B, and C only on those traits without adding new arguments.
4. Reveal Meaning — Reconnect each letter to its option and notice what truly changed the ranking.
win: A, B, and C changed or kept their ranking based on time, fit, reliability, or learning rather than identity.
supports:
• Choose your own measure; notice hidden differences.
• Use your own timeline; do one action for your life.
• Limit social media exposure; return to your priorities.
• Check your own progress; name one thing already working.
• Use your own priorities; track progress by your values.

• Protect one focus block; take a short break.

title: WHEN DOES THIS INFORMATION EXPIRE?
goal: Mark old information as expired instead of letting it keep voting in the current decision.
steps:
1. Picture Expiry — For each influential input, picture an expiry condition: price changes, role ends, policy updates, health status shifts, deadline passes.
2. Expire Old Data — Notice any expired item. Stop letting it guide new behaviour until the information is refreshed.
win: At least one influential input received an expiry condition and stopped guiding behaviour once it was stale.
supports:
• Mute alerts; park secondary tasks.
• Close extra tabs; reduce nearby noise.
• Return after interruptions; use a short focus block.
• Take a real screen break; return to one target.
• Close what you do not need; use one screen.

title: QUARANTINE THE UNAVAILABLE VARIABLE
goal: Park a problem whose key variable is unavailable until the condition for useful processing arrives.
steps:
1. Name Variable — Name the exact variable outside present control—another person’s decision, test result, future opening, missing resource.
2. State Change — State what change would make processing useful.
3. Store It Away — Until then, store the problem with that trigger and refuse further computation.
win: The missing decision, result, opening, or resource received a trigger for reopening and no further calculation before then.
supports:
• Take a short break; choose one target.
• Return to one target; use one window at a time.
• Reduce background noise; use one screen.
• Protect one focus block; clear visual clutter.
• Put the phone out of reach; keep one task visible.
formula_flow: Name Variable → State Change → Store It Away
safety:
PAUSE
Continue any preparation that remains possible while the variable is unavailable.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

win: Reason, date, action, review point, and reversal conditions stayed recorded instead of being rebuilt from mood.

title: GIVE THE THOUGHT A RETURN ADDRESS
goal: Route a returning concern to one real destination or mark it undeliverable.
steps:
1. Assign Concern — Assign the concern to one place: a named person, calendar slot, document, task name, or deliberate release.
2. Route Address — Say the address in your mind and route the thought there each time it returns.

title: WANT NOW / PROTECT LATER
goal: Acknowledge what the urge wants now while protecting what future life still needs.
steps:
1. Picture Urge — Picture what the present urge wants, then what future life is worth protecting.
2. Name Cost — Name the cost each imposes on the other.
3. Choose Action — Choose one action that acknowledges desire while keeping the valued asset intact.
win: The chosen move made room for desire without sacrificing the longer-term asset you named.
supports:
• Leave the trigger; remember urges peak and fall.
• Ride the peak; change rooms if possible.
• Keep your hands busy; eat or drink if hunger matters.
• Drink some water; use your hands.
• Delay ten minutes; make access harder.
formula_flow: Picture Urge → Name Cost → Choose Action
safety:
PAUSE
Seek support when cravings threaten safety, sobriety, or financial control.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT KIND OF EFFORT IS THIS?
goal: Identify what kind of effort you are feeling before deciding that effort means failure.
steps:
1. Use Evidence — Classify the strain using evidence.
2. Stop Novelty — If danger, stop; if novelty, allow learning; if skill growth, dose it; if poor design, simplify the system.
3. Respond Category — Respond to the category instead of interpreting all effort as failure.
win: Danger, novelty, skill growth, or poor design each received a different response instead of one global verdict.
supports:
• Add small friction; change the environment.
• Move the cue; notice the trigger.
• Reset without self-criticism; delay the routine.
• Replace one response; make the new habit easier.
• Change the environment first; keep replacement easy.

title: PREVIEW THE AFTER
goal: Picture the ten seconds after completion clearly enough to make the first move easier.
steps:
1. Protect Enjoyed — Picture a ten-second scene immediately after completion: what is lighter, available, learned, protected, or enjoyed.
2. Include Sensory — Include a sensory marker plus one practical consequence.
3. State Accessible — Begin the task while that specific after-state remains accessible.
win: A sensory after-scene and one practical benefit stayed available while the task began.
supports:
• Name today's date; notice room temperature.
• Feel your feet; reduce sensory input if needed.
• Notice where your body is supported; hear one real sound.
• Feel the chair; notice temperature and texture.
• Notice three colours; keep your eyes on something steady.
formula_flow: Protect Enjoyed → Include Sensory → State Accessible
safety:
PAUSE
Do not fabricate benefits that the action is unlikely to deliver.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: FIND YOUR WORKING GEAR
goal: Find a work-rest gear that matches actual strain instead of your prediction about strain.
steps:
1. Run Pulse — Choose one ordinary task and run it for exactly thirty seconds without trying to finish it.
2. Full Stop — Stop completely for fifteen seconds. Hands off, eyes away, and no planning the next move.
3. Read Strain — Rate actual strain as light, workable, heavy, or stop. Compare it with what you predicted before starting.
4. Set Gear — Choose the next gear—30/15, 60/30, or stop—and complete exactly one more cycle at that ratio.
win: A short work cycle with a deliberate ending revealed whether the next ratio should increase, hold, or finish.
supports:
• Use a visible cue; choose a rough beginning.
• Skip extra setup; shrink the first action.
• Make it visible; open the task.
• Open only what you need; restart quickly.
• Make the first move tiny; lower standards briefly.
formula_flow: Run Pulse → Full Stop → Read Strain → Set Gear
safety:
PAUSE
Stop for pain, illness, exhaustion, agitation, compulsive timing, or any task where interruptions create safety risk.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE BORING DOSE
goal: Practise a small, fixed dose of boredom without adding stimulation or extending the challenge.
steps:
1. Choose Boring — Choose a safe boring task and decide on ten slow breaths.
2. Remove Extras Mentally — Decide that no extra stimulation will be added during those breaths.
3. Stay — Notice boredom’s body sensations until the tenth breath.
4. End Cleanly — Stop there, even if you could continue; increase future doses slowly.
win: Ten slow breaths passed with the boring task unchanged, and the exercise stopped exactly at the planned dose.
supports:
• Use ordinary surroundings; unclench your jaw and shoulders.
• Wait out the surge; keep movements gentle.
• Stay somewhere physically safe; reduce caffeine.
• Let breathing stay natural; look at ordinary objects nearby.
• Reduce extra stimulation; loosen your shoulders.
formula_flow: Choose Boring → Remove Extras Mentally → Stay → End Cleanly
safety:
PAUSE
Adapt for attention disorders and never use boredom as punishment.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

goal: Use concrete evidence of past progress to justify the next realistic step.
steps:
1. Create Prior — Collect three concrete differences created by prior effort—speed, quality, recovery time, knowledge, frequency, distance.
2. Date Examples — Attach dates or examples.

win: Three dated differences made one currently doable action feel earned by evidence rather than optimism.

• Start with one minute; lower the first demand.
• Make the first move tiny; use one window.

title: WHAT SPECIES OF UNKNOWN IS THIS?
goal: Match each kind of unknown with the strategy that actually fits it.
steps:
1. Classify — Categorise the unknown: answerable now, answerable later, influenceable but unknowable, or permanently unknowable.
2. Apply Move — Match it with research, scheduling, influence, or acceptance.
3. Use Category — Refuse to use one category’s strategy on another.
win: Answerable-now, answerable-later, influenceable, and permanently unknowable questions stopped borrowing each other's solutions.
supports:
• Accept a small margin of risk; use a decision deadline.
• Limit checking; accept small risk.
• Stop reopening choices; delay reassurance.
• Leave one question unanswered; set a limit on checking.
• Ask what is controllable now; act with uncertainty.

safety:
PAUSE
Reclassify when access to information or influence changes.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THREE RINGS OF AGENCY
goal: Act where you have control, ask where you have influence, and release what you can only watch.
steps:
1. Imagine Three Rings — Imagine three rings: CONTROL, INFLUENCE, WATCH.
2. Place Each Part — Put each piece of the problem in the right ring in your mind.
3. Take Action — Do one thing you control, make one request where you have influence, and let go of one thing you can only watch.
win: One controlled action, one influence request, and one watched item each landed in the ring where they belonged.
supports:
• Act with uncertainty; choose good enough.
• Use a decision deadline; accept a small margin of risk.
• Stop reopening choices; act on the safest workable option.
• Notice when checking stops helping; delay reassurance seeking.
• Avoid reopening settled choices; leave one doubt.
formula_flow: Imagine Three Rings → Place Each Part → Take Action
safety:
PAUSE
Observation still requires protective action when risk indicators appear.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE UNANSWERED URGE EXPERIMENT
goal: Delay one answer-seeking urge and watch whether the need for information survives the wait.
steps:
1. Question Demands — When the question demands an answer, picture it and delay asking for a short, chosen interval.
2. Track Urge — Track urge intensity at beginning, middle, and end without researching.
3. Decide Afterward — Decide afterward whether information is still needed for action or only for relief.
win: The urge was tracked from beginning to end without research, then information was judged by action need rather than relief.
supports:
• Use a deadline; accept small risk.
• Choose good enough; act on the safest workable option.
• Delay reassurance; leave one doubt.
• Delay reassurance seeking; limit checking.
• Choose a good-enough option; name what is unknown.
formula_flow: Question Demands → Track Urge → Decide Afterward
safety:
PAUSE
Do not delay answers required for health, safety, or deadlines.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

PAUSE

title: FIVE CLUES MAY BE ONE CLUE
goal: Collapse repeated clues that all came from the same source before judging how much evidence you have.
steps:
1. Name Clues — Name up to five clues currently supporting the worried conclusion.
2. Link Sources — Imagine a line between clues that came from the same person, event, article, assumption, mood, or repeated retelling.
3. Collapse Copies — Collapse every linked cluster into one source family; do not count its echoes separately.
4. Recheck Claim — Recheck the claim using the number and quality of independent families that remain.
win: Echoes from one person, event, article, assumption, mood, or retelling became a single source family.
supports:
• Make the old habit harder; keep replacement easy.
• Expect slips and restart quickly; use the same replacement repeatedly.
• Delay the routine; make the new habit easier.
• Change one cue; reset after slips.
• Remove easy access; change the environment.
formula_flow: Name Clues → Link Sources → Collapse Copies → Recheck Claim
safety:
PAUSE
Do not collapse separate danger signs or ignore qualified medical, legal, financial, or safety evidence.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

GOAL
Collapse repeated clues that all came from the same source before judging how much evidence you have.

HOW TO PLAY
1. Name Clues — Name up to five clues currently supporting the worried conclusion.

3. Collapse Copies — Collapse every linked cluster into one source family; do not count its echoes separately.
4. Recheck Claim — Recheck the claim using the number and quality of independent families that remain.

WIN
Echoes from one person, event, article, assumption, mood, or retelling became a single source family.

• Remove easy access; change the environment.

title: ONE LOCAL REASON
goal: Find one reason within the next day that deserves ten minutes of your behaviour.
steps:
1. Find Anchor — Search only within the next twenty-four hours for one person, place, promise, task, or act that matters.
2. Name Reason — Name why it matters locally.
3. Invest Time — Give it ten minutes of undivided behaviour.
win: A nearby person, place, promise, task, or act received undivided time because its local meaning was clear.
supports:
• Rest before deciding; check basic needs.
• Avoid decisions at peak emotion; delay the message.
• Lower nearby noise; check the facts separately.
• Give the feeling time to move; use plain language.
• Separate feeling from fact; name the emotion.

safety:
PAUSE
Seek urgent help if meaninglessness includes suicidal thinking.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

GOAL
Find one reason within the next day that deserves ten minutes of your behaviour.

1. Find Anchor — Search only within the next twenty-four hours for one person, place, promise, task, or act that matters.

3. Invest Time — Give it ten minutes of undivided behaviour.

WIN
A nearby person, place, promise, task, or act received undivided time because its local meaning was clear.

• Rest before deciding; check basic needs.

• Lower nearby noise; check the facts separately.
• Give the feeling time to move; use plain language.
• Separate feeling from fact; name the emotion.

Meaning does not always arrive as a life purpose. One small reason can be enough to organise the next ten minutes.

title: GIVE THE BIG QUESTION A ROOM, NOT THE HOUSE
goal: Give a big question a limited thinking room, then return the rest of the day to living.
steps:
1. Set the Room — Choose a short time for the big question.
2. Bring One Question — Think about one clear question and stop when the time ends. You do not require a final answer.
3. Return To Life — Then do one normal task that shows how you want to live now.
win: The inquiry stopped on time without a final answer and one ordinary action resumed afterward.
supports:
• Reduce easy access to triggers; expect slips and restart quickly.
• Reset after slips; make the old habit harder.
• Change one cue; keep replacement easy.
• Change the environment first; remove easy access.
• Move the cue; interrupt the usual sequence.

title: MOVE THE VALUE TO A NEW VESSEL
goal: Move the value tied to a loss into a new honest channel without calling it a replacement.
steps:
1. Name Lost — Name what the lost person, role, place, or ability allowed you to express—care, mastery, belonging, beauty, service.
2. Find Different — Find a different, honest channel for a small portion of that value.
3. Start — Begin without treating substitution as replacement.
win: Care, mastery, belonging, beauty, or service found one small new vessel while the original loss stayed acknowledged.
supports:
• Name today's value; use values to choose trade-offs.
• Choose aligned action; act before motivation.
• Name what matters today; check whose goal you are chasing.
• Check whose goal; review what the action costs.
• Use one priority; accept the trade-off.

title: BUILD MEANING ON FIVE LEGS
goal: Strengthen one weak source of meaning without asking the strongest source to carry everything.
steps:
1. Rate Meaning — Rate meaning currently available through relationship, contribution, growth, experience, and transcendence.
2. Choose Weakest — Choose the weakest repairable leg and one small action that strengthens it.
3. Keep Strongest — Keep the strongest leg from carrying everything.
win: Relationship, contribution, growth, experience, or transcendence gained one small action where repair was possible.
supports:
• Start with one minute; begin while unsure.
• Remove one obvious distraction; use two minutes.
• Lower standards briefly; cut the task.
• Start before you feel ready; choose a rough beginning.
• Set a two-minute timer; touch the first item.

title: MAKE THE ORDINARY WORTHY OF FULL CONTACT
goal: Give one ordinary routine full attention as if its usefulness made it worthy.
steps:
1. Choose Routine — Choose one routine act—making tea, bathing, preparing a child’s bag, opening work.
2. Perform — Do it without rushing or secondary media.
3. Craft — Notice craft, dependence, and life supported by the act.
4. Finish Deserved — Finish as if it deserved completion.
win: A simple act was completed without rushing or secondary media, and the life it supported became visible.
supports:
• Ask what failure would cost; use strongest evidence.
• Keep new facts separate; commit once chosen.
• Reduce the options; set a deadline.
• Stop researching after enough evidence; accept one trade-off.
• Ignore imagined regret; choose the option you can support.

safety:
PAUSE
Keep pace appropriate when practical urgency is real.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THIS IS A CHAPTER, NOT THE BOOK
goal: Put today's event inside a much longer life story instead of making it the title.
steps:
1. Place Today — Position today’s event on a long timeline with past chapters already survived and blank space ahead.
2. Picture Future — Picture three future signposts that remain possible but unknown.
3. Choose Sentence — Choose one sentence describing this chapter accurately without making it the title of the whole life.
win: Past chapters, unknown future signposts, and one accurate chapter sentence restored scale around the present event.
supports:
• Look for one missing fact; use a real example.
• Separate possibility from probability; question absolute words.
• Add the missing context; check the whole situation.
• Use recent, concrete evidence; avoid treating guesses as facts.
• Delay major conclusions when upset; ask what else could fit.
formula_flow: Place Today → Picture Future → Choose Sentence
safety:
PAUSE
Avoid future projection when immediate crisis requires present support.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: CHANGE THE MENTAL TOOL, NOT THE PRESSURE
goal: Use the mental mode that matches the actual demand instead of applying pressure with the wrong tool.
steps:
1. Decide Accept — Classify the demand as SOLVE, DECIDE, FEEL, ACCEPT, COMMUNICATE, or WAIT.
2. Name Mode — Name the mode currently running.
3. Choose Shut — Shut it down and do the first action belonging to the correct mode—calculate, choose, allow, release, speak, or schedule.
win: Solve, decide, feel, accept, communicate, or wait was identified and the first matching action replaced the mismatched mode.
supports:
• Use one window; set a two-minute timer.
• Lower standards briefly; start smaller.
• Make it visible; lower the first demand.
• Skip extra setup; cut the task.
• Start before you feel ready; shrink the first action.
formula_flow: Decide Accept → Name Mode → Choose Shut
safety:
PAUSE
Mixed situations may need modes in sequence rather than one label.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: WHAT PREPARATION DID WORRY ACTUALLY PRODUCE?
goal: Separate the preparation worry produced from the simulation it keeps repeating.
steps:

win: Any real gap was prepared once; when no gap remained, further worry lost its claim to useful work.
supports:
• Begin with the easiest part; start with one minute.
• Set a two-minute timer; skip extra setup.
• Open the task; remove one barrier.
• Prepare the task in advance; use a visible cue.
• Lower standards briefly; start physically.

title: NAME THE GUARANTEE YOU ARE SECRETLY BUYING
goal: Name the emotional guarantee you hope checking will buy, then ask whether data can actually sell it.
steps:
1. Finish Sentence — Finish this sentence: ‘If I keep checking, I hope to guarantee that…’ Ask whether any amount of data can provide that emotional promise.
2. Remain Demand — Gather only information that changes action; treat the remaining demand as uncertainty to carry.
win: Only information that could change action remained; the impossible guarantee was recognised as uncertainty to carry.
supports:
• Choose good enough; accept a small margin of risk.
• Choose a good-enough option; act with uncertainty.
• Delay reassurance; name what is unknown.
• Leave one question unanswered; use a decision deadline.
• Avoid reopening settled choices; accept small risk.
formula_flow: Finish Sentence → Remain Demand
safety:
PAUSE
Do not stop investigation while essential facts are still obtainable.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: THE TURNING POINT AT HALF SPEED
goal: Replay only the turning point slowly enough to keep observation separate from motive.
steps:
1. Recall Exchange — Choose no more than ten seconds of the interaction, beginning before the moment that felt different.
2. Halve Speed — Run those ten seconds once in imagination at half speed. Keep only what you can actually observe: words, pauses, volume, face, and movement.
3. Shift — Stop at the first change and name it without motive: ‘the pause lengthened,’ ‘the volume rose,’ or ‘the reply shortened.’
4. Keep Fact — Keep that one fact. End the review before building another explanation.
win: One visible change—pause, volume, face, movement, or reply length—was kept while the review ended before explanation multiplied.
supports:
• Start physically; lower the quality bar.
• Use a visible cue; enter through easy work.
• Lower standards briefly; touch the first item.
• Choose tiny action; make it visible.
• Start before you feel ready; stop planning after one action.
formula_flow: Recall Exchange → Halve Speed → Shift → Keep Fact
safety:
PAUSE
Stop if this review raises distress, becomes compulsive, or concerns abuse or danger that requires support and protection.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

goal: Let the best-supported thought advise the decision instead of giving every thought an equal vote.

1. Score Evidence — For each influential thought, score evidence, relevant expertise, recency, and decision relevance.

win: Evidence, expertise, recency, and relevance changed the ranking while weaker voices stayed recorded but nonbinding.

• Remove one obvious distraction; use a visible cue.

title: TURN THE LOOP INTO FIVE ICONS
goal: Turn a repetitive thought loop into simple images and interrupt the first repeated meaning.
steps:
1. No Sentences — Imagine five boxes. Do not use full sentences.
2. Imagine Five Signs — Give each of the last five thought turns one simple inner picture.
3. Spot The Return — Notice the first picture whose meaning comes back later.
4. Choose An Exit — At the next box, picture one real fact to check or one small action to take, then stop imagining.
win: The first returning icon exposed the loop, then one real fact or action replaced another thought turn.
supports:
• Name one useful action; use your hands.
• Stop solving the unsolvable; do something that needs your hands.
• Shift attention outward; set a clear stopping point.
• Ask if any new information exists; name one action.
• Limit how long you review it; end the replay.
formula_flow: No Sentences → Imagine Five Signs → Spot The Return → Choose An Exit
safety:
PAUSE
Do not imagine this while driving; stop if the mental sequence becomes compulsive, perfectionistic, or more distressing than the thought.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.

title: DEMOTE THE HEADLINE EXPERIENCE
goal: Give the dominant thought or sensation equal status with three background details.
steps:
1. Hold Sensation — Hold the dominant sensation or thought with three background what you notices—one sound, one contact point, one visual feature.
2. Give Attention — For a contained interval, give all four equal attentional weight without imagining a separate watcher.
3. Demote the Headline — Notice how centrality changes.
win: Sound, contact, vision, and the headline experience shared attention, changing which one felt central.
supports:
• Return attention to the room; use fewer words about it.
• Notice the thought; return to the room.
• Stop debating; drop the need to solve it.
• Drop the explanation; use fewer words.
• Use present facts; avoid building a larger story.

safety:
PAUSE
Stop equalisation when one signal requires urgent priority.
This is a self-help exercise, not emergency or medical care.
